t.krasnoe selo@59.7,30.1:
Readers of Anna Karenina will know Krasnoye Selo, even if they have never been within a thousand kilometres of it. It was here, at the summer camp of the imperial guards, that Tolstoy set the officers' steeplechase in which Vronsky rides his mare Frou-Frou to disaster in front of the court. For more than a century, from the early nineteenth century until the revolution, the guards regiments of the Russian army gathered each summer in this area south-west of Saint Petersburg for manoeuvres, parades and horse races, and the tsar and the court came to watch. It is listed as one of the monuments associated with the historic centre of Saint Petersburg.

Today Krasnoye Selo is a district of the city, with apartment blocks, old churches and parks, and the traces of the imperial camp are scattered and subtle. The town lies at the foot of the Duderhof heights, a ridge of hills that is the highest ground in the surroundings of Saint Petersburg, with views on clear days across the flat land toward the Gulf of Finland and the city. During the Second World War the front line of the siege of Leningrad ran through this area, and the heights saw heavy fighting.

The riding around Krasnoye Selo is mostly flat, with long straight roads, some busy traffic close to the city and quieter lanes as you head out toward Ropsha, Gatchina and the villages of the Leningrad region. Road surfaces vary, with potholes and patched sections not unusual, and the weather is changeable, with short, bright summers and long, dark, cold winters. Summer nights around the solstice barely get dark at all.

As a sizeable suburban district, Krasnoye Selo has petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés in easy reach. Within reach are the imperial palaces of Peterhof, with its fountains, and Gatchina, as well as the palace and park at Ropsha. Saint Petersburg itself, with its canals, museums and bridges, is less than an hour away.

The countryside here has a melancholy beauty: birch woods, wet meadows, small lakes and the wide sky of the north. Come in early summer, when the white nights are at their brightest and the air smells of lilac and cut grass, and remember that a whole imperial court once came here to watch officers race their horses.
t.tallinskoe highway@59.8,30.2:
Not every historic road is a pretty one, and the Tallinn highway on the south-western edge of St Petersburg is not trying to win prizes for charm. It is, however, one of the old imperial routes out of the capital, the road toward Narva and Reval, today's Tallinn, and as such it forms part of the UNESCO listing of the historic centre of St Petersburg and its related monuments, which includes the network of roads tying the city to its palaces and estates. Along it, the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries planted suburban residences, military camps and post stations.

The districts around here, Uritsk, Sosnovaya Polyana and Gorelovo, are now part of the city's sprawl, with Soviet apartment blocks, shopping centres and tram lines. But the land has a hard history. During the siege of Leningrad from 1941 to 1944, the German front line ran close by, and Uritsk and the Ligovo area were scenes of savage fighting. Memorials along the roads mark the positions. Further south-west, Krasnoye Selo was the summer camp where the imperial guard held its manoeuvres, and the Duderhof heights rise above the flat land as the first real hills you meet leaving the city.

Riding here is about getting somewhere rather than enjoying the journey for its own sake. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, surfaces can be rough, with potholes and tram rails to cross at angles, and the weather is unpredictable, from summer heat to sudden cold rain blowing off the Gulf of Finland. White nights in June bring an endless dusk that makes evening rides feel unreal, while winter is no season for two wheels at all. Toward Peterhof and Strelna, the roads become greener, lined with parks and the remains of noble estates.

Fuel, food and repairs are easy to find around Uritsk and along the main roads. If you are heading toward the palaces of Peterhof, Oranienbaum or Ropsha, this is the logical route out, and cafés along the way serve blini, soups and strong tea. Bear in mind the current difficulties of travel to Russia for many foreign riders and check the rules carefully. As for the road itself, ride it with a little imagination: beneath the asphalt and traffic lights lies a route once travelled by couriers, generals and emperors.
t.church of archangelos michael@35.0,32.8:
From the outside, the church of the Archangel Michael at Pedoulas looks like a barn, with a steep wooden roof covered in flat tiles coming almost to the ground. Inside, its walls are covered with frescoes painted in 1474 by a local artist named Minas, with bright colours and lively scenes from the life of Christ and the saints, and the archangel himself presiding over the door. It is one of the painted churches in the Troodos region listed by UNESCO, a group of small Byzantine churches and monasteries whose humble exteriors hide some of the richest interiors in the Eastern Christian world.

Pedoulas is a village in the Marathasa valley, high in the Troodos mountains, at over a thousand metres. It is known for its cherries, which ripen in early summer, and for its cool air, a relief from the heat of the plains. The valley is steep and green, with terraces, orchards and pine forests. Kykkos monastery, the richest in Cyprus, lies a short ride away, and Mount Olympus, the highest point on the island at almost two thousand metres, rises to the east, with a ski area in winter. Kakopetria, in the next valley, has an old quarter of stone houses along the river.

The riding in the Troodos is outstanding. The roads climb from the plains through endless hairpins, with pine forests, villages and views over the island to the sea. Surfaces are mostly sound, and traffic is light except on weekends, when Cypriots head to the mountains. Remember that Cyprus drives on the left. Watch for gravel, fallen rocks, goats and cyclists. Summer is hot on the plains but pleasant in the mountains; winter can bring snow and ice on the high roads.

Pedoulas has small shops, cafés and tavernas, and Kakopetria has more choice; fuel is available in some villages, but stations are spread out, so fill up when you can. Cypriot food is generous: meze, a long procession of small dishes, souvla, grilled meat on skewers, halloumi and local wines from the mountain villages. Ask at the village for the key if the church is closed, step inside, and let your eyes adjust to the colours; after the dark wooden roof, the frescoes glow.
t.prioratsky park@59.6,30.1:
Gatchina has a palace that most visitors head for first, but the building that makes riders and architects alike stop and stare is the little Priory Palace standing on the shore of Black Lake in Prioratsky Park. It looks like a small Gothic castle with a tower and a chapel, pale and slightly unreal against the water, and it is built of rammed earth. Nikolai Lvov, the architect and polymath, put it up around 1799 for Emperor Paul I, who had made himself Grand Master of the Knights of Malta and wanted a residence to offer the Order. The earth walls, compacted in layers and then plastered, have now survived more than two centuries of Russian winters, which is a better record than plenty of brick.

The park around it is wilder than the formal gardens of the Great Palace, with lakes, wooded islands and paths that wander off into marsh and birch. Gatchina itself, about forty kilometres south of St Petersburg, was Paul's favourite residence before he became emperor, a place where he drilled his troops in Prussian style and built himself a private world away from his mother Catherine's court. The town suffered badly under German occupation in the Second World War, and much of what you see has been painstakingly restored.

Getting here is easy, which is both the blessing and the curse. The main roads out of the city are busy and straight, with heavy trucks and impatient drivers, so the pleasure lies in the side routes. The Gostilitsy road heads northwest across the low Izhora Upland through forest and farmland, with gentle rises, the occasional long bend and villages strung along the way. Expect patchy asphalt, sudden potholes and the odd unmarked level crossing, and treat any wet surface in spring with care. Early mornings at weekends are calmer, and the late light of June turns the lakes to silver.

As a stop, it works very well. Gatchina is a proper town of nearly ninety thousand people, so fuel, cafés, pharmacies and supermarkets are all a few minutes away, and there is parking near the park entrances. Walk the short loop around Black Lake, look closely at the walls of the priory where the plaster has been cut back to show the earth beneath, and then decide whether you have time for the Great Palace as well. You probably do not, and that is fine.
t.peterhofskaya road@59.8,30.2:
Peterhofskaya Road was once the grandest road out of St Petersburg. Running southwest from the city along the shore of the Gulf of Finland toward Strelna and Peterhof, it was lined in the eighteenth century with country estates, dachas and palaces built by the nobility, who wanted to be close to the imperial residences along the coast. Peter the Great started the trend, granting plots to courtiers along the road, and the result was a chain of estates with gardens, parks and ponds stretching for miles. Many of these estates survive in some form, and the road and its surroundings are part of the UNESCO listing of the historic centre of St Petersburg and related groups of monuments.

The area around Sosnovaya Polyana and Uritsk, now part of the city's southwestern suburbs, was on the front line during the siege of Leningrad in the Second World War, and the German army was dug in only a few kilometres from the city centre. Much of the area was destroyed, and the estates suffered badly. Today, the landscape is a mix of Soviet apartment blocks, parks, and the remnants of old estates, with some restored and others in ruins. Further west, the Konstantinovsky Palace at Strelna has been restored as a state residence, and Peterhof, with its fountains, is one of Russia's most famous sights.

Riding along the Peterhof road is more of a historical journey than a pleasure ride. The road is busy, with heavy traffic, trams and traffic lights, and the surface can be rough in places. But as you move west, past Strelna, the views open up toward the Gulf of Finland, and the parks and palaces become more frequent. Summer, with its white nights, is the best time to ride, when the light lasts almost all night and the parks are green. Winter brings snow, ice and short days.

The southwestern suburbs of St Petersburg have every service, including a filling station, somewhere to eat and shops. Try Russian dishes such as blini, pancakes with sour cream or caviar, and pelmeni, dumplings filled with meat. Stop at one of the old estate parks along the road, take a walk among the trees, and imagine the carriages rolling along the road to Peterhof. Then continue west to Strelna and Peterhof to see the palaces in their full glory.
t.pulkovskaya observatory@59.8,30.3:
On the Pulkovo heights, the low ridge south of St Petersburg, an observatory has been watching the sky since 1839. It was founded by Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve, the German-born astronomer who became its first director, and it quickly became one of the leading observatories in the world, with the largest refracting telescope of its day. The Pulkovo meridian, running through the observatory's main building, served as the reference for Russian maps for many years. Struve also led the measurement of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a chain of survey triangulations stretching from the Arctic Ocean to the Black Sea, which helped determine the size and shape of the earth and is now a UNESCO site.

The observatory was destroyed during the Second World War, when the Pulkovo heights were on the front line of the siege of Leningrad. The Germans shelled the area heavily, and the buildings were reduced to ruins, though some instruments and the library had been evacuated. After the war, the observatory was rebuilt and reopened in 1954, and today it is still an active research institute, with telescopes, a museum, and guided tours. The grounds, with their alleys of trees and white buildings, have a calm, academic feel.

Riding up to Pulkovo is easy, as it lies close to the city, just south of Pulkovo airport, along the Pulkovskoye highway, which carries heavy traffic. The ridge offers views over the city, and on a clear day you can see the domes and spires of St Petersburg on the horizon. The surrounding area has a mix of suburbs, fields and monuments to the defenders of Leningrad, and the roads to Pushkin, a short ride to the southeast, with its Catherine Palace and the famous Amber Room, are more pleasant. Weather can be grey and damp much of the year, but the summer white nights are magical.

Shushary and Pushkin, nearby, have petrol, coffee and proper meals, and the city has everything. Pushkin is a great place for a meal and a walk in the palace parks. Visit the observatory museum if you can, look at the telescopes, and stand on the heights looking north toward the city. It is a place where science and war have both left their mark, and where the stars still draw people's attention.
t.the ensemble of the zinoviev s datcha@59:
Here the Neva is a working river, broad and fast, carrying barges and the outflow of Lake Ladoga past factories and housing blocks on its way to the city. Yet on the left bank near Ust-Izhora, among the industry, survive the traces of a much older riverside life: the country houses, datchas in the old aristocratic sense, that Saint Petersburg's wealthy families built along the Neva in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with parks running down to the water. The ensemble of the Zinoviev datcha is one of them, included in the long list of estates, parks and buildings that make up the World Heritage Site around the historic centre of Saint Petersburg. I would not promise much in the way of restored splendour; come for the river and the layers of history.

The deepest layer is medieval. In July 1240, at the mouth of the Izhora where it enters the Neva, Prince Alexander of Novgorod surprised and defeated a Swedish force. The victory earned him the name Nevsky, and he became one of Russia's most venerated saints and national heroes; Peter the Great later had his relics moved to the monastery he founded in the new capital. A church dedicated to Alexander stands at Ust-Izhora, and the village holds re-enactments and commemorations around the anniversary.

The riding here is honest about what it is: a busy main road along the river, industrial suburbs, trucks heading for the ring road, potholes and tram tracks closer to the city. It makes sense as part of a route along the Neva towards Shlisselburg and the fortress of Oreshek at the river's source, where the Neva leaves Lake Ladoga, rather than as a destination in its own right. Weather in this region swings from humid summer heat to long, dark, icy winters, and the riding season is short.

Foreign travel to Russia is heavily restricted in practice for most Western riders at present, with sanctions and insurance and payment problems on top of visas, so official advice should be the first thing you check.

Metallostroy, four kilometres away, is a sizeable industrial town with fuel and shops, and the city itself is a short ride downstream. Smoked fish, sold at roadside stalls along the river and the lake, makes an excellent snack.
t.the palace and park of the mikhailovskay:
Carlo Rossi did not design a palace so much as a piece of a city. Between 1819 and 1825 he built the Mikhailovsky Palace for Grand Duke Mikhail Pavlovich, younger brother of Alexander I, and at the same time laid out the square in front of it and the streets leading to it, so that the façades all answer one another. Today the palace houses the Russian Museum, which holds one of the greatest collections of Russian art anywhere, from medieval icons through Repin's huge canvases to Malevich and the avant-garde. Behind it the Mikhailovsky Garden runs down to the Moika, shaded and calm in the middle of the city.

Next door, the Church of the Saviour on Spilled Blood, all onion domes and coloured tiles, marks the spot on the Griboyedov Canal where Emperor Alexander II was mortally wounded by a bomb in 1881. Between the church, the garden, the Field of Mars and the Summer Garden, this is one of the loveliest walks in Saint Petersburg, and all of it lies within the World Heritage Site of the historic centre.

Riding in the city centre has one rule that matters more than any other. From spring to autumn the bridges over the Neva are raised at night to let ships through, typically for several hours after midnight, and if you are on the wrong island when they go up, you wait. Locals plan whole evenings around the timetable; you should too. Beyond that, expect heavy traffic, cobbles and tram rails near the canals, hard-to-find parking and drivers who treat lane markings as suggestions.

Whether you should be riding here at all right now is a question for official travel advice: sanctions and practical barriers have made Russia very difficult for most Western visitors since 2022.

Fuel is available everywhere in a city of five million, though less so in the historic core itself. Saint Petersburg eats well, and Georgian restaurants, with khachapuri cheese bread and khinkali dumplings, are as much a part of the city's food culture as Russian ones. After the museum, sit in the garden by the Moika and watch the tourist boats slide under the bridges.
t.highway pushkin gatchina@59.6,30.3:
Two imperial palaces lie at either end of this road, and between them the flat country south of Saint Petersburg still carries the scars of the twentieth century's worst siege. At the northern end is Pushkin, the former Tsarskoye Selo, where the Catherine Palace stretches its blue and white façade for hundreds of metres and the reconstructed Amber Room glows inside. At the southern end is Gatchina, Paul I's palace, grey and fortress-like, in a park of lakes and islands. The historic road between them is one of the many components of the World Heritage Site of the historic centre of Saint Petersburg and its related monuments.

From September 1941 the German siege ring around Leningrad ran through these southern suburbs. Pushkin and Gatchina were occupied, the palaces looted and burned, and the Amber Room carried off, never to be found. The defenders' lines are marked today by memorials of the Green Belt of Glory, a chain of monuments along the former front, and the rides that pass here link several of them. Standing among birch trees beside a memorial, with traffic hissing past, it is hard to imagine nearly nine hundred days of hunger and shelling, but the names and dates make you try.

The road itself is a modern highway, flat and fairly straight, crossing fields, woods and the edges of towns like Kommunar, an industrial town on the Izhora. It is busy, with commuter and truck traffic and some fast, impatient driving, and the surface varies from new asphalt to tired patchwork. In autumn the birch woods turn bright yellow, and in winter the whole country is white and the roads are icy for months.

Western riders face a different obstacle first: since 2022 sanctions, visa and insurance problems have made Russia extremely hard to visit, and many governments advise against travel, so check before you plan.

Kommunar, eight kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and both palace towns have plenty of cafés. Give yourself time at Gatchina in particular; its park is far less crowded than Pushkin's, and its lakes, bridges and grottoes are a quiet place to think about everything this road has seen.
t.petrovsky@59.9,30.1:
The coordinates put you on the edge of the Neva Bay, west of the old fishing village of Lakhta, where the northern shore of the Gulf of Finland meets the sprawl of St Petersburg. The label is a puzzle: Petrovsky could refer to any of a dozen places in a city named after Peter the Great, and it is safest to treat it as a viewpoint on his great project, the opening of Russia to the sea. Whatever the exact spot, the landscape is unmistakable: flat shore, reeds, wide grey water, and on the horizon the dome of the Kronstadt cathedral and the line of the flood barrier.

This stretch of coast has changed enormously in recent years. The Lakhta Center, a glass skyscraper more than four hundred and sixty metres tall, rises from the shore, the tallest building in Europe, twisting upward like a flame. Nearby is the Gazprom Arena stadium on Krestovsky Island, and the Western High-Speed Diameter, an elevated toll motorway, sweeps along the coast on huge bridges. It is a modern city's face, very different from the baroque palaces of the centre.

The bay itself was the stage for much of Peter's work. He founded the city in 1703 at the mouth of the Neva, built forts in the water to protect it from the Swedes, and laid out estates and palaces along both shores. The southern shore became the imperial coast of Peterhof and Oranienbaum; the northern shore remained wilder, with fishing villages and later dachas. The riding today is urban and suburban. The Primorsky prospekt and the coastal road leading northwest towards Olgino and Sestroretsk are busy, with traffic lights and heavy congestion at peak hours. The toll motorway is fast and offers impressive views over the bay, but it is a motorway, nothing more. Further north, around Sestroretsk and Lake Razliv, the roads become pleasant, with pine forest and lakes.

The weather on the gulf is changeable. Wind off the water can be cold even in summer, and rain arrives quickly. White nights in June make for long, luminous evenings.

There is fuel and everything else in the surrounding districts. Before planning a trip, check current entry requirements and travel advice for Russia carefully, and expect foreign payment cards not to work.
t.ayios ionannis@35.0,32.8:
Ayios Ionannis here means the monastery of Saint John Lambadistis, at Kalopanagiotis, a village in the Marathasa valley on the northern side of the Troodos mountains. It is a strange and lovely building, three churches joined together under one big wooden roof, each added in a different century, so that stepping from one to the next is like walking through the history of Cypriot painting. Frescoes cover nearly every wall, from the Byzantine saints of the twelfth century to the more elaborate cycles of the fifteenth, in colours that glow in the dim light. It is one of the painted churches of the Troodos, listed by UNESCO in 1985.

The village itself is a bonus. Kalopanagiotis sits beside a stream among plane trees and orchards, and it has sulphur springs that have been used for healing since the Middle Ages, with a small spa in the old style. In summer people come from the coast for cool air, and in the cafes on the main street they sell sweet preserves of fruit and nuts, called glyka tou koutaliou. Kakopetria, a bigger village further down the valley, is full of old stone houses and also has a painted church of its own.

The riding in the Marathasa valley is among the best on the island. The road follows the river upstream from the plain through terraces of cherry and apple, with sharp bends, long climbs and views of dark, forested ridges. Surfaces are generally good, though shaded stretches can stay damp, and in autumn fallen leaves make corners slick. Weekend traffic includes cyclists and tourists, so go early. Leave time for a lunch of grilled halloumi, lamb baked in a clay oven and fresh bread in a village taverna.

Fuel in the valley is limited, so fill the tank before you leave the larger towns, such as Limassol or Nicosia, though a small pump may exist in a bigger village. Spring brings blossom, and summers are warm in the day and cool at night, with the high ground often fresher than the coast by ten degrees. Winter brings snow and closures on the highest roads, but the valley is usually open, and the smoky smell of village fires gives the air a welcome richness.
t.the palace and park of the znamenskaya d:
South-west of Saint Petersburg, along the shore of the Gulf of Finland, the land is a continuous belt of imperial estates. Peterhof is the best known, with its gilded fountains and long terraces, but behind it and around it is a countryside of parks, dachas and country palaces built by the imperial family and the aristocracy from the eighteenth century onward. Znamenka was one of these. The name comes from the Znamenie, the Sign, and the estate had a palace and a park that served as a summer residence, laid out in the landscape style that was fashionable in the nineteenth century. I cannot tell you what condition it is in today, and I would rather not describe rooms I have not seen.

The country around is flat, wooded and damp, with birch, alder, ponds and the occasional long avenue of old lime trees. The land is only a few metres above sea level, and the Baltic light is soft and silvery, with long dusk in summer and the famous white nights in June, when it never gets fully dark. In winter, the snow lies deep, and the gulf freezes at the edges.

Riding here is a matter of surfaces and traffic. The highways around Peterhof and Strelna are busy with lorries and commuter cars, and the old roads between the estates are patched and rutted, with frost heave in spring. The best time of day is early morning in summer, when the roads are empty and the parks are cool. The Kievskoe highway named in the ride titles is a main road, so expect trucks. Peterhof is a town of over seventy thousand, so fuel and food are easy there, and Strelna and Ol'gino are smaller.

For anyone planning a trip, the practical side of travel in this region has changed a great deal in recent years, and the rules on entry and on bringing a motorcycle are the first things to check. If you can go, the combination of landscape parks, fountains and the gulf makes a day worth having. A walk in the park, with the smell of damp leaves and the sound of rooks in the tall trees, is the best thing here.
t.the otdelny park@59.7,30.4:
Pavlovsk and Pushkin sit side by side on the plain south of Saint Petersburg, and both grew from the imperial taste for country palaces. Pushkin was once Tsarskoye Selo, the Tsar's Village, where Catherine the Great had a palace of blue and white with a facade that stretches for hundreds of metres, and where the Amber Room once stood. Pavlovsk was a smaller palace for her son Paul, set in one of the largest landscape parks in Europe. The Otdelny Park lies in this region, among the parks and estates, and I cannot say precisely what it contains. The name means separate or detached, and it points to a part of the landscape set apart from the main royal grounds.

Tsarskoye Selo is where Russia's first railway opened in 1837, connecting it with Saint Petersburg, and it is where the poet Alexander Pushkin studied at the Lyceum as a boy, which is why the town now bears his name. The park around the Catherine Palace is full of ponds, pavilions and artificial ruins, built to look like ancient monuments in a painter's view. The estates nearby, including the one in the ride titles, belonged to noble families and officers who built villas around the court.

The riding is flat and slow. Roads around Pushkin and Pavlovsk are busy, with commuter traffic, bus lanes and city potholes, and the best time to go is a summer morning before the tour groups arrive. The parks are beautiful in September, when the birches turn yellow. Pushkin has almost ninety thousand people, so fuel and food are easy, and Pavlovsk has its own cafes near the park gate.

Anyone planning to ride here should check the current rules for visitors and vehicles, since they have changed in recent years and I cannot vouch for today's situation. If the trip is possible, walk in the park and notice how much effort went into making an artificial landscape look natural. The sound of rooks, the smell of leaf mould, and the long straight avenues of lime trees give a particular atmosphere, calm and a little melancholy.
t.the palace and park ensembles of the tow:
Between 1941 and 1944 Tsarskoye Selo lay behind German lines, and when the Red Army came back the Catherine Palace was a shell. The Amber Room's panels had vanished, the park trees had been cut for firewood, and most of the interiors were ash. The restoration that followed, and the new Amber Room that finally reopened in 2003, make this one of the most remarkable rebuilding jobs in Europe. The town, now called Pushkin after the poet who studied at its Lyceum, is part of the UNESCO listing for the historic centre of Saint Petersburg, and the ensemble of palaces, pavilions and parks around it is the reason to come.

The Catherine Palace is the great blue and white pile with a gilded line of ornament along the roofline, and the park beside it is a landscape of lakes, bridges and mock ruins that cost an empire's worth of money to arrange. A short walk away stands the Alexander Palace, a plainer, neoclassical house where the last tsar's family lived before the revolution, and its park is quieter and more rural. These coordinates fall closer to the countryside south of the town, near Aleksandrovskaya, where the land is flat and wooded and the suburbs thin out into fields.

For the ride, expect flat country, wide roads and busy ones. The approaches from the city carry commuter traffic and lorries, and the surface alternates between good asphalt and frost-heaved patches. Nobody comes here for corners. Come for early morning in summer or for late September, when the birches go yellow and the parks are nearly empty. In midsummer the white nights keep the sky light until almost dawn, and a late evening in the park is a surprisingly good time.

Pushkin has some ninety thousand people, so fuel, cafes and supermarkets are plentiful, while the smaller settlements around have little. Allow a couple of hours for the palace, which draws long queues at weekends, and bring cash for the entrance. Given how much has changed in the region in recent years, check the current rules for visitors and vehicles before you plan a trip, because I cannot vouch for the present situation.
t.church of ayios nikolaos@35.0,32.9:
Above the village of Kakopetria, on the slopes of the Troodos mountains in the middle of Cyprus, the Church of Ayios Nikolaos stands under a roof of its own. The name Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis means Saint Nicholas of the Roof, and the explanation is simple: the little Byzantine church was so precious, and the Troodos winters so wet, that a second, steeply pitched timber roof with tiles was built over the original to protect it. The church dates from around the eleventh century, and inside its walls are covered in frescoes from several different periods, from the Byzantine to the later Middle Ages.

It is one of ten painted churches of the Troodos that UNESCO listed together in 1985, and the paintings are what you come for. The figures of saints and scenes from the life of Christ are painted in earth colours, red, ochre and deep blue, and the effect in the half-light is intimate and strangely moving. The church is a working place of worship, so dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, and be quiet. A custodian is usually on hand, and if the door is locked there is normally a number to call.

For riders, the Troodos is the best reason to visit Cyprus. The roads climb from the plain through pine forest, with long, flowing curves, tight hairpins and shaded stretches that smell of resin. The surface is mostly good, but gravel and a few potholes appear on the minor roads. Remember that traffic in Cyprus drives on the left. Weekends bring many cyclists and day-trippers, and mornings are quietest. Snow can fall on the upper slopes from December to March, and Mount Olympus, at 1,952 metres, sometimes has skiing.

Kakopetria is a village with a well-preserved old quarter of stone houses and wooden balconies, a stream, and trout restaurants along the water. It has cafes and a shop, and probably a fuel pump, though Lefka, fifteen kilometres away, is a larger town with a certain supply. In the villages around, you can find local halloumi, honey and carob syrup, and in the autumn, the grape harvest and the sweet wine of the area, including Commandaria, are worth tasting.
t.scientific town institution of physiolog:
Ivan Pavlov did not do his best-known work in a lab in a big city. The Russian physiologist, who won the Nobel Prize in 1904 for his research on digestion and who became famous for the experiments on conditioned reflexes in dogs, spent his last years at Koltushi, a village on the low hills east of St Petersburg. Here, from the early 1930s, the Soviet state built him a whole scientific town, with laboratories, kennels, a monkey station and housing for his staff, in the hope that he would turn out a physiology of the mind. Pavlov, who lived from 1849 to 1936, said he wanted a place where animals and people could be studied in healthy conditions and surrounded by nature, and Koltushi was it.

The institute still stands, and the village has kept its name in the history of science. Pavlov was a difficult man, an old-fashioned Russian intellectual who disliked the Bolsheviks and said so, yet he was allowed to carry on, and the place became a kind of scientific island. There is a memorial and a small museum devoted to him and the work done here.

Koltushi lies on the road to Lake Ladoga, and the connection is not coincidental. In the siege of Leningrad in 1941-44, the only route that kept the city supplied was the Road of Life, an ice road across Ladoga in winter and a ferry line in summer, and the villages east of the city, like this one, were the staging posts. Memorials line the route, with stone markers numbered by kilometre. The landscape is flat and wooded, with birch and pine forest, marshes and farm clearings, a typical north Russian plain, and the light in early summer, with its long white nights, is soft and gold.

I should add a plain note on the practical side. Travel in Russia for riders from Europe and many other countries has become complicated, with visa rules, insurance problems and restrictions on foreign vehicles, as well as official travel warnings, so check the current position well before planning anything. In normal times the roads around St Petersburg are busy and fast, with heavy trucks, a lot of roadworks and a rough surface in places. Koltushi and neighbouring Staraya have a few thousand people each, with fuel and shops available in the area, and the city itself is a short run away.
t.historical centre of the town of gatchin:
Gatchina is the kind of town you reach by flat, straight Ingrian roads, and the first impression is of birch, pine and wide skies rather than anything dramatic. Forty-odd kilometres south-west of St Petersburg, it sits on land that was once swampy and sparsely settled, until the eighteenth century decided otherwise. Catherine the Great gave the estate to her favourite Grigory Orlov, and the architect Antonio Rinaldi built him a severe, castle-like palace of local limestone beside a lake. After Orlov died it passed to her son Paul, who made it his private kingdom, drilled his soldiers on the parade ground and added the odd fortress-style touches that suited his nature.

The palace is the reason people come, but the whole historical centre is worth a slow loop. The park around it is full of water: the White Lake, island pavilions, hidden bridges and a priory built from earth and stone, which is a peculiar thing to find in a Russian park. Gatchina was occupied in the Second World War and the palace was gutted, so what you see has been rebuilt over decades from photographs and fragments. That makes the finished rooms feel earned rather than inherited.

For a rider this is a town stop, and it is a good one. With almost ninety thousand people there is fuel on the main approaches, plenty of cafes and shops, and room to park near the park gates without drama. The roads in from the Petersburg side are busy and often rutted at the edges after winter, so give yourself margin, particularly in the wet. Cobbled stretches in the old quarter are rough and slippery after rain, and trams or lorries leave little forgiveness.

The best time is a clear morning in late spring or early autumn, when the light on the pale walls is soft and the lake is quiet. Summer weekends bring tour buses and local families, and winter turns the whole approach to ice for months, which is not motorcycle weather. If you are heading on towards Babolovo and the other parks that ring the city, the countryside stays gentle and green, a low rolling landscape of fields, wet woods and old estate roads. It is not twisty, but it is rich in stories, and Gatchina tells the loudest of them.
t.railway saint petersburg pavlovsk@59.8,3:
Pavlovsk station has a story that every Russian railway enthusiast can tell. The line from Saint Petersburg to Tsarskoye Selo opened in the late 1830s, the first public railway in the country, and it was soon extended to Pavlovsk, where a grand station building became a place of concerts and summer entertainment. Johann Strauss the younger came to conduct there in the nineteenth century, and the rich of the capital rode out in their finery to hear him. The railway still runs, though the trains are electric and the concert hall has long gone quiet.

The coordinates here are on the southern edge of Saint Petersburg, near Shushary, a place that has grown from a village into a sprawling suburb of tower blocks beside the Moscow highway. The old line runs through flat land of fields, woodland and big industrial estates. It is not scenic in the usual sense, but it has a history written into it, in cuttings and embankments, level crossings and old brick station houses.

Riding here means dealing with city traffic. The roads south of the city are busy, with trucks heading for the ring road and the Moscow highway, and the surface is often rutted and patched. Intersections are crowded, and a rider should keep a careful eye on the lane ahead. A short way on, the countryside opens out, and the lanes around Pavlovsk are a pleasant contrast, with old villas among birch and pine.

Fuel is easy. Shushary has stations along the main roads, and the town of Pushkin, only a short ride away, has everything. For a coffee, look for the small bakeries and cafes near the railway stations, which tend to be cheap and cheerful.

The best time to come is early summer, when the long light makes even a suburban edge glow, or the early weeks of autumn, when the park trees turn yellow. Winter is dark, cold and icy, and not the season for exploring.

A short ride from here you can reach the great park at Pavlovsk, one of the loveliest landscape gardens in Russia, and the rail line is a handy guide to it.
t.the park mariental@59.7,30.5:
Pavlovsk's great park spreads over several hundred hectares along the Slavyanka river, a valley of meadows, groves and winding water that was designed as a landscape garden for the family of Tsar Paul I, with the palace by the Scottish architect Charles Cameron as its centrepiece. The name Mariental, meaning Maria's valley, recalls the empress Maria Feodorovna, who spent decades shaping the grounds after her husband's death. Little of it was left in 1944, when the retreating German army burned the palace and felled thousands of trees, and its restoration after the war took years of patient work.

What you find today is a green and peaceful place, full of old oaks, silver birches and lime avenues, with pavilions, bridges and statues half hidden among the trees. The paths are good for walking, and cyclists share them. Dogs, children and joggers fill the park on summer weekends. In autumn the leaves make a coloured carpet, and in winter, when snow covers the ground, the place is almost magical.

The town of Pavlovsk, with about sixteen thousand inhabitants, lies right next to the park and has fuel, bakeries and cafes. The road to it from Pushkin, which is only a few kilometres off, is short and straight, with the odd bend where an old villa stands. Parking at the park gates can be crowded on weekends, so go early. The surface in town is patchy, and the traffic slow.

Do not expect a thrilling ride. This is a place for taking things slowly: parking the bike, walking in the shade and thinking about the history of the place. The riding comes in the lanes between Pavlovsk and neighbouring Tyarlevo, where birch woods and meadows give a taste of rural Ingria, the old name for this part of Russia.

The park is at its best in late May, when the trees are in leaf and the birdsong is loud, and again in September and early October, when the light is golden. Mosquitoes can be thick in July, so carry repellent. Winters are long, snowy and cold, and the roads can be icy.
t.historical centre of the town of pushkin:
The history of the Pushkin district begins with a Swedish manor and a Russian victory, and the story of what grew there is the story of the Russian court itself. The town was long called Tsarskoye Selo, the Tsar's Village, and the great Catherine Palace, with its long blue and white facade and gilded decoration, was the summer residence of the empresses. Inside, the Amber Room, once panelled with amber, was looted during the Second World War and has been recreated in recent decades, to the delight of visitors.

The town was renamed Pushkin in 1937, to mark the centenary of the poet's death, who had studied at the Lyceum here as a boy. The school building still stands next to the palace, and the park behind it is full of memories of his poems. The historic centre, with the palace, the Alexander Palace, the Catherine Park and its lakes, is listed by UNESCO together with Saint Petersburg.

With nearly ninety-three thousand inhabitants, Pushkin is a proper town with every service a rider might need. The main road from Saint Petersburg is busy, and traffic builds up at the palace in summer, with tour buses jostling for space. Parking close to the palace is limited and often restricted, so look for a side street or one of the signed car parks. The streets of the old centre are narrow and the surfaces uneven, with a few cobbled stretches that need a careful hand.

Ride in on a weekday morning in May or September, and you will find the town at its best. The park is quiet, the long avenues of lime and maple are in leaf, and the light on the palace is soft. At weekends, and in the high summer, the crowds can be dense. The cafes near the park serve good pastries and strong coffee, and a plate of blini is a classic accompaniment.

Winter is cold and snowy, and the park looks beautiful under a blanket of white, but the roads can be treacherous, with black ice on the bends and snow banks along the verges. Dress warmly, and take care.
t.moskovskaya road@59.9,30.3:
Moskovsky Prospekt is the long, straight avenue that runs south from the heart of Saint Petersburg towards Moscow, and the road you are on is the oldest piece of the highway that links the two capitals. The first paved road between them was laid in the early nineteenth century, a line of stone and gravel across marsh and forest, and it still carries the traffic that gives the two cities their rhythm. The city that lines it is a very different Saint Petersburg from the one on the postcards: wide streets, heavy Stalinist buildings and long perspectives of tower blocks.

A little way along, the avenue passes the Moscow Triumphal Gate, an iron monument built in the 1830s to celebrate the Russian army's victories, and then runs past Victory Square, with its monument to the defenders of Leningrad. The siege of the city by the German army lasted almost nine hundred days, from 1941 to 1944, and the front line ran close to the southern suburbs. Further south, the Pulkovo Heights, where the observatory stands, were a battlefield. Their history is present in every monument along the road.

For a motorcyclist this is a place to pass through rather than to linger. The avenue is wide, busy and full of traffic lights, and trams run in the middle of it in some sections. Cobbles and tram lines can be slippery in the wet, and drivers are fast and aggressive. Fuel is plentiful, with stations on every main road in Kupchino and Avtovo, districts of around fifty thousand people each, and cafes and shops at every corner.

Come early in the morning to avoid the worst of the traffic, and keep to the left lanes if you intend to pass through. Summer evenings are mild and light, while in winter the road is salted, black and wet, and the grit on the surface is hard on the tyres.

If you have time, look for the old milestones and the little parks along the avenue, where the city's past peeks out from behind the concrete.
t.the menagerie@59.7,30.5:
Pavlovsk is the least showy of the great palaces around St Petersburg, and for that reason the pleasantest. The estate lies a few kilometres from Pushkin, on the Slavyanka river, in a park that spreads over hundreds of hectares of woodland, meadow and winding water. Catherine the Great gave the land to her son Paul in 1777, and the Scottish architect Charles Cameron, later joined by Brenna and others, gave it its look, with pavilions, bridges and a colonnaded Temple of Friendship set among the trees. The Menagerie in this label is one of the corners of that landscape, an old estate feature whose exact surviving form I would not describe in detail, but the surrounding park is real and beautiful.

Getting there from the city is straightforward but not scenic: you ride south out of St Petersburg on the Moskovskoye highway through suburbs, retail parks and the grey skirt of Pushkin, then turn off into Pavlovsk, where speed limits drop and the lanes narrow. Pavlovsk station is itself a piece of history, since the Tsarskoye Selo railway of 1837, the first in Russia, ran here and the station became a concert hall where Johann Strauss played summer seasons. Tyarlevo, three kilometres away, is a village and has little to offer beyond the usual shop.

The park rewards a slow walk after you park the bike near the entrance. The beech and lime avenues turn gold in late September, and the whole place feels like an English landscape garden done by someone with Russian space to play with. In the soft light of the white nights, May to July, you can stay until late. Winter transforms it into ski tracks, with locals gliding along the paths on cross-country skis.

Pavlovsk town has about sixteen thousand people, which is enough for fuel, a supermarket and cafes, though you will find larger choice in Pushkin just up the road. Be aware that the palace itself was burnt and looted during the war and restored over many years, so the interiors you see are largely a post-war act of devotion. Traffic into the city on the way back can be heavy on Friday and Sunday evenings, so leave early or very late.
t.saint petersburg@59.9,30.3:
Saint Petersburg was a swamp when Peter the Great decided to build a capital on it. In 1703 he founded a fortress on an island in the mouth of the Neva, on land that belonged to Sweden and had been taken in war, and he forced tens of thousands of workers to drain and pile the marshy ground, thousands dying in the process. Within a few decades the city stood as a European capital, with straight avenues, canals, palaces and a harbour, a window cut, as Pushkin said, to Europe. The Neva delta, with its islands, branches and canals, gave the city a character that is still something between Amsterdam and Venice.

The site is low and flat, and it floods. The Neva has risen many times when westerly storms push the Baltic up the river, most dramatically in 1824, when the water covered much of the city. A long barrier, the dam across the Gulf of Finland that carries the ring road, was completed in the 2010s to protect the city, and it is a surprising structure, a long line over the water with gates for ships. The ring road itself is the fastest way round the city, but it is busy and best avoided at rush hour.

Riding in Saint Petersburg is much like riding in any big city: heavy traffic, trams, potholes, aggressive drivers and the occasional deep pothole on the cobbles. Parking can be a puzzle. The city has plenty of fuel, repair shops and bike dealers, and its sheer size, with over five million people, means anything you need is within reach. Summer is the season, when the white nights from late May to mid-July keep the sky light until midnight and the drawbridges rise in the small hours, a spectacle that draws crowds on the embankments.

At the moment, foreign visitors will find travel to and in Russia heavily restricted, with sanctions, insurance and border problems, so check carefully before you plan a trip.

Food is a delight: blini with caviar or sour cream, pelmeni dumplings, rich soups such as ukha and solyanka, and the pastries sold in the old cafes along Nevsky Prospect. Winter is long, dark and cold, and the Neva freezes, though the city has a beauty of its own in snow. If you can, see the city from the water, on a canal boat, since that is how it was designed to be seen.
t.schlisselburg old ladoga and new ladoga:
The fortress at Shlisselburg is built on an island in the river, at the very spot where the Neva leaves Lake Ladoga, and whoever held it held the water road between the Baltic and the heart of Russia. The Novgorodians built the first wooden walls in 1323, and called the place Oreshek, which means little nut, after the island's shape. Over the next four centuries it passed between Russians and Swedes, until in 1702 Peter the Great stormed it on his way to the sea, and renamed it Schlusselburg, the key fortress, a key that would unlock the Baltic. Within a year he had founded Saint Petersburg downstream.

Later the fortress became a prison, and a grim one, reserved for political prisoners. Revolutionaries, rebels and, in 1887, a young man called Alexander Ulyanov, who was hanged here for plotting to kill the tsar, passed through its walls. He was Lenin's older brother. The red brick towers and thick walls are still standing, with a museum and the ruins of the prison, and the island is reached by a small ferry from the town.

The label ties Schlisselburg with Old Ladoga and New Ladoga, and the three places form a group on a tentative heritage list around the southern shore of Lake Ladoga. Old Ladoga, up the Volkhov river, is one of the oldest settlements in Russia, associated in the chronicles with the arrival of Rurik, the half-legendary Viking founder of the Russian line, in the 860s, and has a stone fortress and a twelfth-century church with medieval frescoes. New Ladoga, at the mouth of the Volkhov, grew up around a canal that Peter built to bypass the stormy lake.

The town of Shlisselburg, with about twelve thousand people, has fuel and food. The road from Saint Petersburg runs east along the Neva, flat and straight, a ride of an hour, with frequent speed cameras. Lake Ladoga is the biggest in Europe, and its shore, with reeds, sandbars and pine forest, is wide and cold.

Best visited between May and September, when the ferry runs regularly. Summers are cool, with fog and sudden storms. For travellers, entry conditions to Russia are currently difficult, and I would check before planning. Ask for smoked fish from the lake, such as vendace or bream, at a stall near the harbour.
t.nyamata@-2.1,30.1:
The church at Nyamata is a plain brick building with a corrugated iron roof, and what it holds is the memory of one of the worst weeks of the twentieth century. In April 1994, during the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, thousands of people from the surrounding villages took refuge in the church, as they had in earlier waves of violence, assuming that a house of God would protect them. It did not. Killers entered with grenades, machetes and clubs, and in the days that followed some ten thousand people died in and around the church. Today it is a memorial. The clothes of the victims lie in piles on the pews, the altar cloth is still stained, and in an underground vault the remains of tens of thousands from the district are kept in coffins and on shelves.

I am telling you this plainly because the place deserves plain words. Nyamata is one of four genocide memorials, with Murambi, Bisesero and the one in Kigali, that UNESCO added to the World Heritage list in 2023. It is a place to go with respect, to be quiet, and to listen to the guides, many of whom are survivors.

The setting is the Bugesera, a low, dry region of hills and wetlands south of Kigali, with lakes and papyrus swamps, fields of cassava, banana groves and small farms. Kigali, with three quarters of a million people, is about twenty kilometres away, and has all the fuel, repair shops and hotels you could need. Nyamata itself is a busy town with petrol stations, shops and cafes.

Riding in Rwanda is easier than many expect. Roads are generally well surfaced, traffic is orderly, and helmets are required for riders and passengers. Motorbike taxis, motos, are everywhere, and drivers are used to bikes. Watch for pedestrians, cyclists with huge loads and goats. The dry seasons, June to September and December to February, are best, and rain can come hard in March to May.

Dress modestly and ask before photographing inside the church. Photography is often restricted, and it is better to leave the camera in the bag. The memorial is free, though donations are welcome. Give yourself an hour, and some quiet time afterwards.
t.sanam@18.5,31.8:
Black pharaohs once ruled Egypt from here. In the eighth century BC the kings of Kush, a kingdom on the Nile in what is now Sudan, marched north and conquered Egypt, founding the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and for about a century they governed from Memphis and Thebes while keeping their homeland capital at Napata, beneath a flat-topped sacred mountain called Jebel Barkal. Sanam, on the Nile near Merowe, was part of that landscape, a place with a temple of Amun built by Taharqa, one of the greatest of the Kushite kings, and a large cemetery that held burials of the kings' families and officials over many generations. The area, with Jebel Barkal and the royal tombs at Nuri and El-Kurru, was listed by UNESCO in 2003 as Gebel Barkal and the Sites of the Napatan Region.

The setting is the great bend of the Nile, where the river swings through the Nubian desert in a long loop, with a green ribbon of date palms and fields on each bank and endless sand and black rock beyond. The fourth cataract, a series of rapids, lies upstream, and the Merowe Dam, completed in 2009, now holds back a large lake. Merowe is the nearest town, with a modest population and basic services, and Karima is a short way away. Villages are mud-brick, with painted doors, and life follows the river.

Riding in Sudan has long been an adventure, with desert roads, heat of forty-five degrees in summer, sandstorms and distances where fuel can be hard to find. At present, though, the situation is very different. Since April 2023, fighting between rival military forces has devastated large parts of the country, and travel for visitors is neither safe nor practical. I would not plan to go. The history is there, and will wait.

If one day conditions improve, the best season would be winter, from November to February, when the days are warm and nights cool. The river is the main attraction, with sunsets over the dunes and the sound of water wheels.

For now, this is a place to read about, and to hope for.
t.goreme national park and the rock sites:
Millions of years ago, two volcanoes, Erciyes and Hasan, covered central Turkey with ash, and the ash hardened into a soft, pale rock called tuff. Then rain and frost and wind went to work for a very long time. They carved the tuff into a landscape of cones, spires, mushrooms and canyons, the fairy chimneys of Cappadocia, in soft shades of cream, pink and apricot. About a thousand metres above sea level, around Goreme, the whole valley seems to have been sculpted by a mad pastry chef.

The soft rock was also easy to dig. From the early centuries of Christianity, monks and villagers carved churches, chapels, monasteries, houses and storerooms into the cliffs and cones, and in the ninth to eleventh centuries they covered the walls with frescoes. At the Goreme Open Air Museum, a cluster of rock-cut churches in a valley, you can see them: the Dark Church, with its vivid blue and red paintings preserved by lack of light, and the Apple Church and the Buckle Church. In hard times the people dug whole underground cities, such as Derinkuyu, with stables, kitchens and chapels, and rolling stone doors to close the passages. UNESCO listed the national park and the rock sites in 1985.

For a rider, Cappadocia is superb. Roads are smooth, wide and almost empty, with long curves between the pinnacles and across the rolling plateau, and views open around every bend. You can ride from valley to valley, to Uchisar with its castle-like rock, to Pasabag with its mushroom chimneys, to Avanos on the Red River, famous for pottery, and to Urgup with its wine cellars. Fuel and food are easy in Nevsehir, Urgup and Goreme, which are well supplied with guesthouses, cave hotels and restaurants.

Go early. At dawn, in good weather, dozens of hot-air balloons rise over the valleys in a silent, colourful crowd, and the low light turns the rock gold. Summer is hot and dry, and winter brings snow, which is beautiful but can make roads icy. Spring and autumn are best.

Try testi kebab, meat and vegetables cooked in a sealed clay pot, cracked open at your table, and a glass of the local white wine, from the Emir grape.
t.subterranean city of kaymakli@38.5,34.8:
Kaymakli sits in the soft volcanic country of Cappadocia, about eleven kilometres from Derinkuyu and eighteen from Nevşehir, and from the road you would never guess what is under your wheels. The village is ordinary: flat-roofed houses, tractors, a few carpet shops. The wonder is below, a city dug downward into tuff, the pale rock that ash from ancient volcanoes pressed into something a person can cut with a hand tool and that hardens with air.

Go in and the scale gets to you in odd ways. Corridors are low enough to make a rider in boots and a jacket walk bent over. Round stone doors, shaped like millstones, can be rolled across a passage from inside and could not be opened from outside. There are wells, ventilation shafts that run down through the levels, stables, storerooms and kitchens whose ceilings are still blackened. Around eight levels are said to exist, and only the upper ones are shown to visitors. Who dug it first is argued over; the habit of hiding underground here goes back many centuries, and Byzantine Christians certainly used these refuges when raiders came through the plateau. Stories of a tunnel linking Kaymakli to Derinkuyu get told with confidence, though nobody has proved them.

The riding around it is gentle, wide and quick on the main roads, with rock chimneys and pigeon-hole cliffs appearing in the fields. Early morning light on the tuff is the best of the day, and tour coaches arrive mid-morning, so you will be glad to be first in the tunnels. Summer on the plateau is hot and dry, spring has green wheat and poppies, and winter can bring real snow at this height, so check the forecast before you set off for the day.

For practicalities, Derinkuyu is a proper town of over twelve thousand people and has fuel and plenty of food, and Nevşehir is bigger still. Between the two there are tea gardens where a glass of çay costs very little. Take a light layer into the underground city, because it stays cool and damp while you sweat outside, and bring a small torch if you want to peer into side passages that the lighting skips.
t.gisozi b@-1.9,30.1:
Gisozi is a hillside district of Kigali, and for most visitors it means the memorial. The Kigali Genocide Memorial, on a ridge in Gisozi, is the burial place of more than two hundred and fifty thousand victims of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, and it also houses a museum that documents the killing, its causes and its aftermath, with photographs, clothing and testimonies. It is sobering, honest and carefully made, and it is the most important stop for anyone who wants to understand modern Rwanda. Allow at least two hours and go with an open heart.

The city around it is something else. Kigali is a place of hills, a green city of well-swept streets and flower beds, spread over ridges at about 1,500 metres, with a mild, dry climate that makes it more comfortable than many equatorial capitals. Plastic bags have been banned since 2008, and on the last Saturday of each month, the community work day called umuganda closes most shops and many roads in the morning while neighbourhoods sweep and repair, so plan your day accordingly.

Riding in Kigali is an acquired skill. Motorcycle taxis, locally called motos, are everywhere, weaving through traffic in numbers, and their riders are required to wear helmets and carry a spare for their passenger. Traffic rules are strictly enforced, with police checkpoints and speed cameras, and the city streets are well paved, though steep, with tight junctions and heavy traffic at rush hours. Roundabouts are busy. Rain brings sudden downpours that turn gutters into streams, so allow a margin on the hills.

Fuel is easy in Kigali, a city of more than seven hundred thousand, with stations on the main avenues, and you will find mechanics for most bikes. For food, brochettes of grilled goat or beef, cooked over charcoal and served with bananas, are the classic, and the local coffee is among Africa's best, with cafés that roast their own beans. The highlands of the country are never far, and an hour's ride takes you into the terraced hills.

Visit the memorial in the morning, when you are fresh, and leave the afternoon for something gentler.
t.gisozi a@-1.9,30.1:
Rwanda's coffee is a good reason to spend an afternoon in Kigali's hills. Gisozi, the district on the northern ridge of the city, is better known for its memorial, but the neighbourhood is also a good base for exploring the city's café culture, since the climate and altitude that make Rwanda a fine place to grow coffee also make it a pleasure to drink it. Arabica bushes, mostly of the bourbon variety, grow on small farms in the volcanic and high-altitude soils of the country, picked by hand and washed at nearby stations, and the beans are known for a bright acidity and notes of fruit and flowers.

Kigali is the capital, set among a series of steep hills and valleys with a population approaching three-quarters of a million. Most of the central roads run along ridge lines, with sudden drops into green valleys on either side, and many of the valleys are wetlands used for small farming. Houses climb the slopes in tight terraces. The result is a city of viewpoints, where at almost any junction you can look out across red-roofed neighbourhoods and eucalyptus groves to the next hill.

For the rider, the pleasure is in the geography. The tarmac is good and well marked, and a short ride out of town leads to roads through tea and banana plantations, with sweeping views, long gradients and few potholes. Speed limits are low and enforced with cameras, so ride within them. Dusk comes at around six all year round, and after dark, unlit pedestrians and bicycles laden with goods make nighttime riding dangerous. Early morning is the best time for a ride, with mist lying in the valleys and the air fresh.

Fuel is found at stations across the city, and the main roads have workshops and tyre shops. Cafés and small restaurants are numerous, with buffets of rice, beans, plantain, cassava leaves and fish from Lake Victoria, and a brochette stand on almost every corner. Some roasteries offer tastings, and buying a bag of beans is a fine way to remember the visit.

Come in the dry months, June to September, when the hills are bright and the roads are clear.
t.church of panayia@35.0,32.9:
The churches of the Troodos mountains look, from outside, like barns. In the high, cool country of the island's interior, where snow can fall in winter, builders covered their churches with a second, steeply pitched timber roof of tiles to protect the older domed buildings underneath, and the result is a plain, sturdy exterior that gives no hint of the paintings within. Inside, walls and ceilings are covered with Byzantine frescoes, some from the eleventh century and later, showing saints, angels and scenes of the life of Christ in rich, deep colours. Ten of these churches are listed by UNESCO.

Kakopetria, a village of about twelve hundred people, is one of the best bases for exploring them. Its old quarter has stone houses with wooden balconies, narrow lanes and a stream, the Karyotis, once used to turn mills and now lined with trout farms and cafés. A little way from the village, the church of Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis, Saint Nicholas of the Roof, is among the listed group and has paintings spanning many centuries. The church of Panayia, the Virgin, which gives this point its name, belongs to the same tradition. Some of the churches are kept locked, so ask in the village for the keyholder, or check the opening times in advance.

The ride up into the Troodos is the reason for coming. From the coastal plains, roads climb through pine and juniper forest, with bends and hairpins, deep valleys and glimpses of the sea. Traffic in Cyprus drives on the left, a legacy of British rule, which is useful to remember at junctions. Surfaces are generally good, though rough at the edges, and the mountain air is cooler than on the coast by several degrees. Winter brings snow and ice to the higher roads, and Mount Olympus, the island's highest point at nearly 1,950 metres, has a small ski area.

Kakopetria has a few shops and cafés, but the larger towns on the coast, such as Limassol, have the main fuel stations, though some stations are found in the hill villages. Local specialities include grilled halloumi, souvlaki and sweet preserves of walnuts and cherries.

Spring, when the hills are green and the cherries are in bloom, is lovely.
t.nicosia@35.2,33.4:
Nicosia is the last divided capital in Europe, and you feel it as soon as you reach the old city. A great ring of Venetian walls, built in the 1560s in the shape of a star with eleven bastions, encloses the centre, and across the middle runs the Green Line, the buffer zone created after the Turkish invasion of 1974. Barbed wire, sandbags and shuttered buildings mark the line in places, and a few crossing points allow pedestrians to pass between the two halves of the city, which is a strangely routine business, with passport checks and a walk down a pedestrian street.

On both sides, the old town is a muddle of lanes, workshops and churches, with Venetian, Ottoman and British layers. A Gothic cathedral built by the Lusignan kings was converted to a mosque, and the Selimiye now dominates the northern side, while the south has Byzantine churches full of icons, a decent archaeological museum, and cafés in restored houses. Food is Mediterranean with a local twist: halloumi grilled or fried, souvla, which is skewered charcoal-grilled meat, stuffed vine leaves, and sweets soaked in syrup. Coffee is Cypriot, strong and sweet, served in tiny cups with the grounds in the bottom.

Cyprus drives on the left, a legacy of British rule, so riders from the continent need to adapt. Nicosia's traffic is intense and fast, with complex roundabouts and little patience, and in the heat of summer it can reach forty degrees by midday. Leaving town is the reward: to the south-west the road rises into the Troodos Mountains, where pine forests, cool air and tight bends lead to villages and painted churches, ten of which are listed by UNESCO for their medieval frescoes. Mount Olympus, the island's highest point at just under two thousand metres, is the summit, and in winter it carries snow and a small ski area.

Fuel is easily found, with stations around the ring road and on every main highway, and prices are moderate. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and wildflowers in March and April. Summers are very hot, and rain is rare between June and September. Take water on every ride, wear ventilated gear and keep to the shade at midday. The old city is a pleasure on foot in the early evening, when shops reopen and the smell of grilled meat drifts through the lanes.
t.blyde river canyon@-24.6,30.8:
Few canyons carry such cheerful names. When Voortrekkers found the river in the 1840s, they had left the Delagoa Bay fever lowlands in sorrow, fearing their leader was dead; they called a stream Treur, meaning mourning, and when they met the party returning safely, the next river became Blyde, meaning joy. The Blyde River Canyon, in Mpumalanga, is the result: a gorge about twenty-five kilometres long and up to seven hundred metres deep, cut into the northern end of the Drakensberg escarpment and clothed in green subtropical vegetation, making it one of the largest green canyons on Earth.

The finish of the Panorama Route is dramatic. Three huge rounded rock pillars, the Three Rondavels, look like African huts built by giants, and the viewpoint is a place to linger. Further south, Bourke's Luck Potholes are cylindrical hollows scoured by whirling water, named after a prospector who staked a claim here during the 1870s gold rush and found nothing, while others found plenty. God's Window and Wonder View look out over the Lowveld, thousands of feet below, and on clear mornings you can see the Kruger National Park in the distance.

The riding is superb. The roads climb out of the Lowveld on smooth tarmac with long sweeping bends and frequent viewpoints, passing waterfalls, pine plantations and tea estates. Abel Erasmus Pass is a good test, and Long Tom Pass, near Lydenburg, is another favourite. Mist is common in the mornings, and summer afternoon thunderstorms can be violent, so start early and keep a close eye on the sky. In winter, from June to August, days are dry and clear but mornings can be cold.

The nearest services are in Graskop, a small, pleasant town with cafes and fuel, and Hoedspruit and Hazyview offer more choice. Entry fees apply at some viewpoints, and local vendors sell crafts at the lay-bys. Watch for monkeys, which are bold, and for minibus taxis that stop without warning. Baboons live in the area, so keep food out of sight. The country is good, and the people friendly.
t.demre@36.2,30.0:
Demre is the modern town on the site of Myra, one of the great cities of ancient Lycia, and it sits in a flat, fertile plain between the Taurus mountains and the Mediterranean on the south coast of Turkey. A great cluster of tomb houses, cut into the cliff face above the old city around the fourth century BC, looks down on the town, their stone fronts carved to imitate wooden buildings, and a large Roman theatre stands at their foot. It is one of the most impressive ancient sites on the coast, and visitors are often surprised at how few people are there.

The town's other claim to fame is Saint Nicholas, the fourth-century bishop of Myra who became the model for Santa Claus. A Byzantine church in the middle of town, restored in the nineteenth century, is said to have housed his tomb, though in 1087 sailors from Bari in Italy took his bones back to their own city, and Venetians claimed the rest. The church is still a pilgrimage destination, with a good deal of tourist traffic, and the fine mosaic floor is worth a look.

The plain around is covered in greenhouses, producing tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers for export. The sight of plastic roofs glinting under the mountains is not romantic but explains the local economy. Beyond the town, a short drive leads to Üçağız and Kekova, where boats take you over sunken ruins of a Lycian city drowned by earthquakes, with stairs and walls visible beneath the clear water.

The D400 is the coast road, and it is a good ride. Between Fethiye and Demre it winds through pine forest and across rocky headlands, with views of turquoise bays, and the bends are frequent and the surface good. Traffic can be heavy in summer, with buses and lorries, and drivers overtake with optimism, so keep your wits about you. In the hot summer months, the best riding is in the early morning or the evening.

Demre has several petrol stations, shops and simple restaurants, and the grilled fish and fresh vegetable dishes are excellent. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and fewer crowds. Orange and lemon trees line the roads, and the scent of citrus blossom in spring is wonderful.
t.kigali@-1.9,30.1:
Rwanda calls itself the land of a thousand hills, and Kigali is draped over a good number of them, at roughly fifteen hundred metres above the sea. The city climbs and drops in short steep pitches, with red-earth lanes running off the tarmac and views across to the next ridge every time you crest a rise. It is clean, notably so, with a monthly community clean-up day and a ban on plastic bags that visitors notice at the airport. The roads are well surfaced, the lane discipline is better than in most capitals in the region, and the air at this altitude is cooler than the equator suggests.

You will be sharing the streets with thousands of moto-taxis, the riders in numbered vests and spare helmets for their passengers. They are a lesson in local riding manners: quick, close, but mostly predictable. Rules about helmets are enforced, and riders here take them seriously. If you are on a foreign bike, sort out your paperwork and insurance ahead of time and carry copies.

The city's history is heavy. In 1994 an estimated eight hundred thousand people were killed in the genocide against the Tutsi over roughly a hundred days, and the memorial at Gisozi tells the story with care. Many visitors spend a morning there before riding anywhere, and it changes how the countryside feels afterwards. Kigali today is also a young, busy place, with cafes serving the country's high-grown coffee and bars where the Primus beer flows on weekends.

From here the Congo Nile route heads west toward Lake Kivu. Leave early, because the road climbs through tea terraces and banana groves, descends to river valleys, and climbs again, with plenty of bends and some slow trucks. Expect cool mornings and afternoon rain in the wet months, March to May and October to November. The dry months from June to September are easiest.
t.gebel barkal and the sites of the napata:
Where the Nile bends through the Nubian desert in northern Sudan, the land goes flat and brown and then suddenly there is Jebel Barkal, a sandstone butte standing alone above the river bank at Karima. The ancient Egyptians believed it was the home of Amun, and when the Kushite kings of Napata conquered Egypt in the eighth century BC and ruled as the twenty-fifth dynasty, they built temples at its foot. The pyramids of the kings stand in a few clusters along this stretch of the river, at El-Kurru and at Nuri, which is where these coordinates lie, close to Kuraymah and Merowe.

The Nuri pyramids are the larger royal cemetery here, with more than twenty steep-sided tombs, including that of Taharqa, the best-known of the Kushite pharaohs. They are smaller and steeper than the pyramids of Giza, built from sandstone blocks that have weathered into rough stepped shapes, and they rise from the desert like ragged teeth. A few have collapsed into piles of rubble. What makes the visit unusual is that you often have the place to yourself, apart from the wind and the sand drifting between the stones.

The riding is simple desert riding: a paved road along the river, with date palms and fields on one side and open sand on the other, broken by villages of mudbrick houses and the occasional checkpoint. Dust and heat are the main challenges. From November to February the days are manageable, and from April to September they are brutal. Fuel is only available in the larger settlements, such as Merowe, so carry a reserve and plenty of water, and plan to refuel whenever you can.

Please note that Sudan has been through serious conflict in recent years, and many roads, towns and sites have been affected. Anyone thinking about riding here should check government travel advice and local conditions carefully before making plans. If you are reading this at home, these pyramids and the butte are still a remarkable chapter of African history: a black Nubian dynasty that ruled Egypt and built its own tombs, in the same style, beside the Nile.
t.kemer@36.6,30.6:
Kemer is a modern resort built on an old pine coast, and what makes it worth knowing is the mountain behind it. A few decades ago it was little more than a fishing village at the foot of the Beydağları range, but tourism has turned it into a lively town of seventeen thousand people with a long pebble beach, a busy marina and hotels from one end of the bay to the other. The setting is spectacular, though, with the dark, steep slopes of the Taurus coming down almost to the water and clouds sitting on the summit of Tahtalı, which at 2,365 metres towers above the town. A cable car climbs to the top of it, and in clear weather you can see across the gulf of Antalya.

The coast road, the D400, runs south from Antalya along the foot of the mountains, and the stretch to Kemer is a pleasant ride, with a smooth surface, open curves and views of the sea. South of Kemer it becomes quieter and more dramatic, running through pine forest and past old harbours and bays. It is at its best in the early morning, before the resort traffic builds, and in spring and autumn, when the heat is mild. In summer, expect traffic jams near the town and a fierce midday sun.

A short way south lie the ruins of Phaselis, an ancient port with three harbours, built among pines beside the sea. It was a Greek colony, later a Lycian and Roman town, and you can wander among its aqueduct, theatre and paved streets, with the water lapping against old stone quays. It is one of the most atmospheric ancient sites on the coast, partly because of the setting, partly because the crowds are modest. Further south still, at Çıralı, natural flames burn out of the rocks of the Chimaera, a phenomenon that has been burning for thousands of years.

Kemer has fuel, supermarkets, a lively seafront and every sort of restaurant. Göynük, a few kilometres to the south, has a pretty canyon and a quieter atmosphere. If you want to swim, the beaches are mostly pebble, and the water is clear and cool. Take sun protection, and drink plenty of water. In autumn the sea is at its warmest, and the roads are at their most enjoyable.
t.antalya@36.9,30.7:
Antalya makes a better end to a long coast ride than most cities deserve. The old harbour at Kaleiçi sits in a small cove below limestone cliffs, with Ottoman wooden houses, Roman walls and a fluted minaret, Yivli Minaret, standing as the symbol of the town. Hadrian's Gate, a triple arch of white marble built to honour the emperor's visit around AD 130, still serves as one of the entrances to the old quarter. King Attalus II of Pergamon founded the city in the second century BC, and its name comes from him, which shows how long people have wanted to live in this sheltered spot between the sea and the snowy Taurus mountains.
