The modern city is huge, with nearly a million people if you count the whole urban area, and the sprawl of apartment blocks, malls and hotels runs for miles along the bay. Arriving by motorbike, you want to approach in the afternoon when the road from the west has already shown its best, then park in the old town and walk. The streets inside Kaleiçi are narrow, with cobbles that are slippery when wet, and many are pedestrian only.

Behind the city the mountains tower, and on a clear winter day you can see snow on the peaks while palms sway in the harbour. The Düden waterfalls drop right into the sea at one end of the bay, and the beaches in both directions are lined with resort hotels. For riders, the roads that climb into the Taurus above Antalya are well worth a day, with long climbs, cool air and pine forest, but expect trucks and tourist coaches on the main routes.

Everything you need is here: fuel stations, bike shops, hotels and restaurants for every budget. Try piyaz, a white bean salad, and then a plate of grilled meatballs, or sit at a harbour cafe with a glass of tea as the sun drops behind the mountains. October and April are the best months, warm but not too hot, while August is blisteringly hot and packed.
t.ahi serefeddin@39.9,32.9:
Ankara is a city of eras laid over each other, and the old quarter around the citadel is where you feel them most. This mosque, named after Ahi Şerefeddin, belongs to the thirteenth-century Seljuk and early Anatolian beylik period in the hilly Ulus district, close to the citadel walls. The name Ahi points to something characteristic of medieval Anatolia: the Ahi brotherhoods, associations of craftsmen and tradesmen that combined guild, charity and a code of honour, and that held real influence in cities where the central power was weak. I can say less about the building than about the neighbourhood, so treat this as a stop for atmosphere.

The old town of Ankara sits on a rocky hill above a flat plain, and the streets climb around the walls past wooden houses, craft workshops and small cafes. From the top of the citadel you look out over a sea of apartment blocks to the hills beyond, and on clear days see the Anıtkabir, the mausoleum of Atatürk, standing on its own rise. Ankara became the capital of the new Turkish republic in 1923, a modest town of dusty streets chosen partly because it was far from the coast, and today it holds more than three and a half million people.

Do not skip the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, a restored Ottoman bazaar near the citadel, which holds a superb collection of Hittite, Phrygian and earlier finds from across the plateau. It makes sense of everything you ride past in the countryside.

Riding in central Ankara is for the patient, with heavy traffic, one-way systems and steep, narrow streets near the citadel, so the best approach is to park and walk. Ride out on a Sunday morning to see the city at its quietest. Fuel and food are everywhere, with simit, the sesame bread rings, sold from carts, and kebab houses in every street. The city sits at about nine hundred metres, so summers are hot and dry but evenings are cool, and winters bring snow and wind. May, June and September are the best months.
t.ankara@39.9,32.9:
Ankara has the reputation of a civil servant's city, grey and rule-bound, and that does it an injustice. It sits on a high, dry plateau at about nine hundred metres, ringed by hills that are green for about six weeks in spring and golden for the rest of the year, and the capital of the Turkish republic since 1923 is full of surprises. The Roman Temple of Augustus, with its walls carrying an inscription in which the emperor describes his own deeds, stands near a mosque in the old quarter. Roman baths, a column and the old citadel sit within walking distance. Over the plain to the south, the Anıtkabir looks down over the city with solemn dignity.

The day out from here heads west to Gordion, the capital of the Phrygians, about ninety kilometres away. This was the kingdom of Midas, the king who, in legend, turned everything he touched to gold. The tumulus over a royal tomb there, dated to around 740 BC, is one of the biggest burial mounds in Anatolia, and you can walk into a tunnel to the wooden chamber at its heart, the oldest standing wooden building known. Gordion was also the place where Alexander the Great is said to have cut the famous knot in 333 BC.

The road west leaves the city on a fast dual carriageway and then settles into steppe riding, with wide-open fields, small villages and a lot of sky. Surfaces are good, wind can be strong, and trucks are the main hazard. In spring the plain turns green and poppies appear along the verges, while in high summer everything bakes and the horizon trembles in the heat.

With three and a half million inhabitants, Ankara offers everything a rider could want: fuel at every junction, bike dealers, hotels and food from street stalls to proper restaurants. Try Ankara tava, a baked dish of lamb and vegetables, and leave room for the city's famous pears. Winters are cold and sometimes snowy, so aim for April to October.
t.sivrihisar ulu mosque@39.5,31.5:
Sivrihisar means pointed fortress, and the name fits: the little town clusters around a rocky crag in the middle of the high, open country west of Ankara, in what used to be the borderland between Phrygia and Galatia. The Ulu Mosque, the great mosque, is the main attraction, a building of the late thirteenth century with a forest of wooden pillars inside holding up a flat timber roof. This style, in which a prayer hall is filled with carved columns and beams rather than stone arches, was common in medieval Anatolia, and only a few good examples survive. The wood is dark with age, the carvings are worn smooth by centuries of touch, and the effect is a hush that feels very different from the grand stone mosques of Istanbul.

Just outside town, the ancient city of Pessinus, at the village of Ballıhisar, was a sacred place of the goddess Cybele in Roman times, and pilgrims came from across the empire to visit her shrine. The ruins include a temple and a theatre, with a modest museum, and the site is often empty. Sivrihisar also holds a popular air festival, with gliders and light aircraft over the plain, taking advantage of the steady winds that blow across the plateau.

The ride into town from Ankara or Eskişehir is straightforward, over a plateau of wheat fields, low ridges and wide skies. Roads are generally good, with long, easy bends, and the main danger is wind and the occasional slow truck. In summer the steppe turns tawny and shimmers with heat, in spring it is green and carpeted with flowers, and in winter snow can close minor roads.

Sivrihisar has about ten thousand people, so there is fuel, a small bazaar, bakeries and tea houses on the main street. The nearest larger towns are a long way off, so fill the tank here. The bakeries sell hot flatbread in the morning, and the tea houses fill up by nine. Spring and early autumn are the best times, with comfortable temperatures and clear air.
t.seronera@-2.4,34.8:
Serengeti means endless plain in the Maasai language, and Seronera is where the plain stops being a word and starts being a place. It is the central hub of the national park, with an airstrip, a ranger post, a visitor centre and lodges, set where the Seronera river threads through a landscape of acacia, rocky outcrops called kopjes and open grass that reaches to the horizon. The park covers about fourteen thousand square kilometres, and this central valley is the best area for cats. Leopards sleep in sausage trees along the river, lions sprawl on the kopjes in the heat, and cheetahs use the long grass to stalk gazelles.

The great migration passes through the wider ecosystem each year, with more than a million wildebeest, accompanied by zebra and gazelle, moving in a loop between Tanzania and Kenya's Maasai Mara in search of fresh grass. Their timing depends on rain, so you cannot guarantee where they will be, but the central plains around Seronera usually hold animals for much of the year. Early mornings and late afternoons are the best time for seeing wildlife, when the light is gold and the animals are active.

On the way in, the route passes the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, with the huge caldera, and the Olduvai Gorge, where Louis and Mary Leakey found early human remains that reshaped our understanding of human origins. The roads inside the parks are mostly gravel and dirt, rough and corrugated in the dry season, and slick with red mud in the wet. Riding a motorcycle in these protected areas is generally not permitted, and wild animals make it unsafe anyway, so this stop is best understood as part of a wider journey with a safari vehicle and a guide.

For practical purposes, think of Seronera as remote. Services are limited, so do not count on fuel or repairs and plan carefully with your operator. Nights are cool at altitude, and the sky, free of any light pollution, is full of stars. The best time for general wildlife is June to October, the dry season, when animals gather near water and the grass is short.
t.shlisselburg@59.9,31.0:
The Neva begins here, in a rush of grey water pouring out of Lake Ladoga, and at its very mouth sits a small island with a fortress on it. That is Oreshek, which the Russians know as Shlisselburg after the town on the bank, and which Swedes called Nöteborg and Novgorodians founded in 1323 as a nut-shaped stronghold guarding the river route to the Baltic. The Swedes took it in 1611, and Peter the Great took it back in 1702 after a short siege, renaming it Schlüsselburg, the key fortress, because whoever held it held the gate to the sea. It was the first step in the campaign that led to Saint Petersburg.

The island later became a prison, and a grim one. Political prisoners, from Decembrists to the revolutionaries of the People's Will, were held in isolated cells there, and Lenin's elder brother Alexander Ulyanov was executed in the fortress in 1887 after a plot against the tsar. Today the fortress is a museum, reached by a small boat from the town pier, with thick brick walls, a ruined cathedral and a sombre memorial. Boats run in the warm months, depending on weather, and Ladoga can be rough, so check before you plan.

The town has another claim on memory. During the siege of Leningrad, German forces took Shlisselburg in 1941 and cut the last land link to the city, leaving Ladoga as the only route. Supplies crossed by boat in summer and over the ice in winter, along the Road of Life, and in January 1943 the Red Army broke through the narrow corridor along the shore. The area around Sinyavino, a few kilometres away, saw some of the bloodiest fighting of the war, and the forests still hold the remains of that struggle. A monument and a museum stand near the road.

Riding here is easy but not exactly scenic. The roads around the town are busy, with trucks bound for the Neva and the industrial sites along the shore, and surfaces are patched. Wind off the lake can be raw even in summer. Late spring and early autumn are quiet, and white nights give the town a pale glow in June.

Fuel, food and shops are available in town, which is large enough for several stations. Expect cheap cafés and simple places to sleep. The old canal and locks, dating from the nineteenth century, are worth a look, since they bypassed the rough water of the lake.
t.the monastery troitse sergieva pustin@59:
On the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, between St Petersburg and Peterhof, the old road runs past a string of palaces and estates that the Russian elite built in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries to be near the sea and the court. Among them, near Strelna, stands the Trinity-Sergius Hermitage, a monastery founded in the eighteenth century as a dependency of the great Trinity Lavra of St Sergius near Moscow. It is part of the wide UNESCO listing of St Petersburg's historic centre and the monuments around it.

The monastery's churches, with their domes, bell tower and pastel-coloured walls, stand in grounds that run down towards the sea, and the complex has been restored since the end of the Soviet period, when it was used for other purposes. Many famous figures of Russian history are buried in its cemetery. Nearby, the Konstantin Palace at Strelna has been rebuilt as a state residence, and Peterhof, with its fountains and golden statues cascading down to the sea, is just a short ride further west. In summer, the gardens of these estates are full of flowers, and the light lingers late into the evening during the white nights.

The road along the gulf, the Peterhof highway, is busy, especially on summer weekends when city dwellers head for the palaces and the beaches. The surface is mostly good but traffic can be dense and impatient, and speed cameras are common. Further west, the coast road towards Lomonosov and beyond becomes quieter, with views across the water to Kronstadt and the long dam that protects St Petersburg from floods, which carries a motorway across the gulf. Winters are long, dark and icy, and the riding season runs roughly from May to September.

Before planning a visit, check current travel advice, as many governments advise against travel to Russia and there are significant practical difficulties for foreign visitors. Fuel stations are common along the main roads, and Strelna and the surrounding towns have shops and cafés. Russian cuisine offers hearty options such as borscht, pelmeni dumplings and blini pancakes with sour cream or caviar, and a stop for tea is never a bad idea after a day on the road.
t.volkhonskoe highway@59.8,30.2:
The Volkhonskoe Highway is not a scenic mountain road but a historic route on the southern edge of Saint Petersburg, running out from the city towards Gorelovo and the old road to Krasnoye Selo. It belongs to the network of eighteenth and nineteenth century highways that linked the capital with the imperial residences and military camps to the south and west, and it is included in the wider protected area of the historic centre of Saint Petersburg and its related monuments. What you see today is a mix of suburban growth, open fields and stretches of tree-lined road, with the ghosts of history underneath.

That history is heavy here. During the Second World War, the front line of the Siege of Leningrad ran very close to this area, along the Pulkovo heights and through the villages to the south west. For almost nine hundred days the city was encircled, and fierce fighting took place across these fields. Memorials and monuments are scattered along the roads, and the landscape still carries traces of trenches and fortifications in places.

Riding here is mostly about connecting the city with the palaces and parks to the south and west, such as Gatchina, with its Prioratsky Palace built of compressed earth, and Peterhof on the Gulf of Finland. The roads are generally flat and straight, with heavy traffic close to the city and a mix of surfaces, from good asphalt to potholed stretches. Drivers can be impatient, and road markings are not always clear, so defensive riding is a good habit. Summer is the riding season, with the white nights of June offering long, light evenings that are a remarkable experience on a bike.

Gorelovo, with over twenty thousand residents, and the larger suburbs nearby have all the services you could need, including fuel, food and shops. The weather can be changeable, with rain likely at any time and temperatures that can be cool even in summer. Winter is long and harsh, with snow and ice making riding impractical for several months. For travellers from abroad, it is worth checking current entry rules and travel advice before planning any ride in Russia, as conditions have changed significantly in recent years.
t.dudergof@59.7,30.1:
South-west of St Petersburg, the flat land of the Neva lowland rises unexpectedly into a pair of wooded hills, the Duderhof heights, the highest ground for many kilometres around. Their name comes from Finnish, and they have long been a landmark, used for military observation since the eighteenth century and as a summer retreat for the people of the capital. In the nineteenth century, the imperial army held its summer manoeuvres around nearby Krasnoye Selo, and the officers' villas and parade grounds became part of the social life of St Petersburg.

During the Second World War, the heights were the scene of bitter fighting during the siege of Leningrad, as German forces captured them in 1941 and used them as an observation post to direct artillery on the city. They were retaken in January 1944 during the offensive that ended the siege, and memorials on the hills commemorate the soldiers who died. Today, the heights are a protected natural area, with forests of spruce, birch and oak, and views over the plain towards the city.

The roads around here are mostly flat and straight, through suburbs, villages and farmland, with heavy traffic near the city. The Duderhof heights offer a few short climbs and curves, and from the top, the views over the plain are impressive. Further afield, the roads along the Gulf of Finland, towards Peterhof and Oranienbaum, offer pleasant riding.

Krasnoye Selo, a few kilometres away, has petrol and shops, and the city itself has the rest. The heights have walking trails through the forest, and the memorials on the hills are a sobering reminder of the siege. The palaces of Peterhof, with their fountains and gardens, and Gatchina, with its park and lakes, are within easy reach. Anyone thinking of travelling here should check current government travel advice, which for many countries advises against all travel to Russia, and consider carefully the legal and practical risks involved.
t.park the menagerie@59.6,30.1:
Gatchina is one of the great imperial estates ringing St Petersburg, and the Menagerie, the Zverinets, is its wild back garden: a large walled tract of forest north of the palace that was laid out in the eighteenth century as a hunting reserve, with deer and other game kept for the court. Today it is mostly woods, ponds and paths, and on a hot day it is the coolest place within reach.

The palace belongs above all to Paul I, the son of Catherine the Great, who was given Gatchina and turned it into a small, drilled, slightly paranoid world of his own, complete with a private army that he paraded in the courtyard. Later Alexander III made it his favourite residence, feeling safer here than in the capital after his father was killed by a bomb. The palace was badly burned during the German occupation and has been restored piece by piece; the lakes, the Silver Lake and the White Lake, and the little pavilions around them are among the prettiest corners of the whole region.

As a riding stop, Gatchina is honest about what it is: a city of nearly ninety thousand people, about forty-five kilometres south of St Petersburg, with everything you need and a fair amount of traffic. The approach from the north on the Kievskoe highway is fast, multi-lane and dull; much nicer is to come cross-country on the smaller roads from Krasnoye Selo or the Pulkovo heights, through villages and fields with the occasional glimpse of an old church. Inside town, cobbles near the palace and tram-era street layouts need care, and parking near the park gates is easy on weekdays, busier at weekends.

Fuel and food are no problem: there are filling stations on every main road, supermarkets, and cafes near the station and the palace. Mariyenburg on the edge of town is a residential district rather than anything else. The Menagerie paths are for walking, not riding, so lock up, take the helmet off and walk ten minutes in. You will hear woodpeckers, see squirrels, perhaps a heron on the pond, and smell pine resin and damp moss, which after a day of exhaust is its own reward.
t.church of stavros@35.0,33.0:
High in the Troodos mountains of Cyprus, in a quiet valley below the village of Platanistasa, stands a small church with a steep, pitched timber roof that comes almost to the ground, making it look more like a barn than a place of worship. This is Stavros tou Agiasmati, the Church of the Holy Cross, and inside it holds some of the finest late Byzantine frescoes on the island, painted in 1494 by Philip Goul, an artist whose name is recorded in a dedicatory inscription. The scenes from the life of Christ and the legend of the True Cross, rich in colour and detail, cover every wall. The church is one of ten painted churches in the Troodos region listed by UNESCO.

The steep roofs, typical of the Troodos churches, were added to protect the buildings from the snow and rain that fall on these mountains in winter, and they also helped to preserve the frescoes inside. Traditionally, the key to Stavros tou Agiasmati is kept in the village, and visitors arrange access with the caretaker or priest; it is worth checking ahead.

The Troodos is a world apart from the beach resorts of the coast. The mountains rise to almost two thousand metres at Mount Olympus, with forests of pine and cedar, terraced vineyards, orchards of apples and cherries, and stone villages clinging to the slopes. The Pitsilia region around Platanistasa is one of the least visited parts of the range, with small villages, old monasteries and spectacular views. Agros, nearby, is known for its rose products, from rosewater to liqueurs, and for its cured meats.

The riding here is fantastic: narrow, twisting mountain roads with countless bends, steep climbs and descents, and very little traffic. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, rockfalls, potholes and sharp drops on the edges. Remember that Cyprus drives on the left. In winter, snow can close roads at higher altitudes, while summer brings heat, though the mountains are cooler than the coast. Kyperounta and Agros have fuel and shops; for more choice, the larger towns of the plain are a good hour away. Try halloumi, the island's famous grilled cheese, souvla, and the sweet dessert wine Commandaria, made in the villages on the southern slopes of the Troodos.
t.the babolovsky park@59.7,30.4:
Inside a ruined palace in a quiet park south of Saint Petersburg sits one of the strangest objects in Russia: a gigantic bath carved from a single block of granite, more than five metres across, made in the early nineteenth century by the stonemason Samson Sukhanov for the Babolovsky palace. The palace, a small Gothic style residence built for Catherine the Great's favourite Prince Potemkin, was later rebuilt and then ruined during the Second World War, but the bath was too heavy to move and remains inside the shell of the building.

The Babolovsky Park lies just west of Pushkin, the town formerly known as Tsarskoye Selo, where the imperial family built the Catherine Palace and the Alexander Palace, and where the Amber Room, lost during the war, was later recreated. The park itself is quieter and wilder than the formal parks of Pushkin, with ponds, woods and paths that wander through birch and pine. It is a good place for a walk away from the crowds.

The roads around Pushkin are busy, suburban and not particularly scenic, with frequent traffic lights and heavy traffic at rush hours. But the parks and palaces make it worth a visit, and the town has a pleasant atmosphere. In winter, snow and ice make riding difficult, and the season for two wheels is effectively late spring to early autumn.

It is hard to picture anyone ever filling it. The tub reads more as a boast in stone, a demonstration of what Russian masons could do with granite, than as somewhere to take a bath.

Pushkin is a sizeable town with plenty of fuel, food and lodging. Western bank cards and many foreign motor policies do not work in Russia at the moment, so anyone coming from abroad needs to sort out cash, cover and the latest government advice long before the trip. The palaces and parks are popular, especially on summer weekends, and early mornings are the quietest. The Lyceum where the poet Alexander Pushkin studied, and after whom the town is named, is in the centre and open to visitors.
t.the palace and park ensemble of the vill:
The village of Taitsy, south of Saint Petersburg near Krasnoye Selo, is home to an estate built in the eighteenth century for the Demidov family, the industrial dynasty whose fortune came from iron and metalworks in the Urals. The classical manor house, attributed to the architect Ivan Starov, stands in a landscape park with ponds and springs, and those springs mattered far beyond the estate: the Taitsy water conduit, built in the eighteenth century, carried water from here to the palaces and fountains of Tsarskoye Selo.

The landscape here is gently rolling, with woods of birch and pine, fields and lakes. Just to the north, the Duderhof heights rise above the flat country around Saint Petersburg, among the highest points in the region, and offered artillery positions during the Second World War. Krasnoye Selo, a town with a long military history as the summer camp of the Imperial Guard, lies eight kilometres away.

The roads here are rural and suburban, mostly flat, with long straights and gentle bends. Surfaces vary, and potholes are common after winter. Traffic is moderate, heavier near the city and on weekends, when Petersburgers head for their dachas. The best riding season is short, from May to September, and white nights in June mean long evenings with light until late.

Taitsy is a good example of how the imperial capital reached out into its hinterland. The noble estates south of the city were not just country houses; they supplied water, timber, food and soldiers, and the roads that link them today follow old routes between palaces, barracks and villages. Riding slowly between Taitsy, Krasnoye Selo and Gatchina, with its own vast palace and park a short way south, gives a sense of that web. The woods smell of resin and wet moss after rain, and in late summer the verges fill with people picking mushrooms and bilberries, buckets in hand.

Krasnoye Selo has fuel and services. If you are riding in from outside the country, read your own foreign ministry's guidance first; the paperwork side of a Russian trip is harder today than the riding. The estate at Taitsy has been in varying states of repair, so check before visiting; the park is pleasant for a walk whatever the condition of the house.
t.koltushskoe highway@59.9,30.6:
East of Saint Petersburg, the Koltushskoe highway runs through suburban sprawl and countryside toward the village of Koltushi, and it belongs to a memorial landscape that ties the whole region together: the Green Belt of Glory, a chain of monuments marking the defensive line around Leningrad during the siege of 1941 to 1944, when nearly nine hundred days of blockade cost the lives of hundreds of thousands of civilians. Monuments, steles and memorials stand along the roads where the front lines and supply routes ran, including the Road of Life across Lake Ladoga.

Koltushi has another claim to fame. The physiologist Ivan Pavlov, famous for his work on conditioned reflexes, built up a scientific research station here from the late 1920s, which became known as the capital of conditioned reflexes, with laboratories, residences and a monument to his famous dogs. The Pavlov Institute still has a presence here.

The roads around Koltushi are a mix of suburban streets, new housing estates and countryside, with lakes and woods. The Koltushi heights offer views over the area. Traffic can be heavy, especially at rush hours, and surfaces vary. It is not a ride for the scenery but for the history, and the memorials along the way are moving.

It helps to stop at one of the memorials and read the names and dates. The blockade line ran in a ring round the city, and this eastern side faced the corridor toward Lake Ladoga, through which food, fuel and evacuees moved across the ice in winter and by boat in summer. In the hardest winter of 1941 to 1942 the daily bread ration fell to a tiny slice, and survivors' diaries describe people walking past the frozen dead in the streets. Families still lay flowers at the monuments on the anniversary of the lifting of the siege each January. The woods and lakes that now hold dachas and new apartment blocks were, eighty years ago, a front line, and that weight sits quietly over a ride that otherwise looks like any suburban road on the city's edge.

Fuel and services are plentiful in Koltushi and nearby Vsevolozhsk. For anyone from abroad the obstacles are bureaucratic rather than physical, with sanctions affecting payments and insurance. The riding season is short, but the June light lasts almost round the clock.
t.dudergofskaya elevation@59.7,30.2:
The land around St Petersburg is almost perfectly flat, so any hill gets noticed. The Duderhof Heights, a pair of wooded hills rising south of the city near Krasnoye Selo, are the highest ground for many kilometres around, with the higher one, Voronya Gora or Crow Hill, reaching a little under two hundred metres above sea level. From the top, on a clear day, you can see the gilded domes of the city and the waters of the Gulf of Finland.

The hills have been a popular place for walks and picnics since the nineteenth century, when Krasnoye Selo was the site of a large military camp where the imperial guard held summer manoeuvres. Tsar Nicholas I and his successors reviewed the troops here, and the area was dotted with officers' dachas. Later, during the Second World War, the heights became one of the key points of the Leningrad front. German forces captured them in 1941 and used them as an observation post and artillery position to bombard the city during the siege, which lasted nearly nine hundred days. They were recaptured in January 1944, during the operation that ended the blockade.

The area is now a nature reserve, with forests of oak, maple and lime that are unusual this far north, along with rare plants and insects. The slopes are steep for this region, and the paths through the woods are pleasant on a summer day.

Riding here means dealing with the traffic of a metropolis. The roads from St Petersburg to Krasnoye Selo and the surrounding towns are busy, with trucks, buses and cars, and the surfaces can be rough, with potholes and tram tracks. Once you are out of the city, the roads become quieter, but still mostly flat and straight. The best season is summer, from June to August, when the white nights bring daylight late into the evening. Winters are long, cold and snowy.

Krasnoye Selo, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, shops and food. The palaces of Peterhof, Strelna and Gatchina are all within easy reach, and the Trinity-Sergius Hermitage, a monastery on the shore of the Gulf of Finland at Strelna, is a peaceful place to visit. Travellers should check current entry, visa and insurance requirements carefully before planning a trip.
t.kievskoe highway@59.7,30.3:
South of Saint Petersburg, the flat, damp plain of Ingria runs off towards Pskov and the old western frontier, and the Kievskoe Highway is the road that heads that way, the route to Kyiv that gave it its name. The coordinates put you near Pushkin, the former Tsarskoe Selo, the Tsar's Village, where the Russian emperors built their summer palaces among parks, ponds and neat avenues of lime trees.

The Catherine Palace, with its long blue-and-white baroque facade, was the work of the Italian architect Rastrelli for the Empress Elizabeth in the 1750s, and the town was renamed in 1937 after the poet Alexander Pushkin, who studied at the Lyceum here. During the Second World War the town was occupied by German forces from 1941 until early 1944, and the palaces were stripped and burned. The famous Amber Room was removed and never recovered, and the palace has since been rebuilt, with a reconstructed amber room completed in 2003. A short drive away, the Pulkovo hill carries an observatory founded in the nineteenth century, and the road passes close to the old defence lines of the siege of Leningrad.

As a ride, this is a flat, straight, busy road, with heavy lorry traffic and plenty of speed cameras, and it is not for enjoying the bends. The better moments are the minor roads through the parks and the villages around Pushkin and Pavlovsk, where birch and pine woods hide old wooden dachas. Winter lasts long here, from November to March, with snow and ice and early darkness, and the white nights of June, when the sky never fully darkens, are the best time to travel, along with the golden September weeks when the leaves turn.

Pushkin, with some ninety thousand people, has fuel and plenty of cafes, and the palace park is a splendid place to rest, with shaded paths, pavilions and a lake with swans, though entry to the palace itself involves long queues in summer. Rules and conditions for foreign travellers in Russia change, so check the current situation before you plan to ride here. For a traditional meal, look for pelmeni, blini with sour cream and strong tea from a samovar.
t.a f orlov s datcha@59.9,30.1:
Strelna lies on the south shore of the Gulf of Finland, on the road to Peterhof, and it is where Peter the Great first thought of building his seaside palace before he settled on the site a few kilometres to the west. The Orlov dacha, which gives this stop its name, belonged to a family that gave Russia several generals and statesmen, but I do not know enough about the building to describe it, so what follows is the country around it.

Strelna's great monument is the Konstantinovsky Palace, begun for Peter and later given to the Grand Duke Konstantin, restored in the early 2000s for the three-hundredth anniversary of Saint Petersburg and now used for official receptions. The park runs down to the water in a series of canals and lime avenues, and the gulf stretches grey and flat beyond. The whole shore was lined with country houses for the nobility, because Peter insisted that the aristocracy should build near his new capital, and the habit of summering on the coast lasted until 1917. Many of the older wooden dachas were burned or bombed in the Second World War, and the area was close to the front line when the Oranienbaum pocket held out to the west.

On two wheels, the Peterhof highway is a broad road along the gulf, often busy, with long straights, roundabouts, and plenty of cars heading for the fountains at Peterhof on summer weekends. It is a good road for steady cruising, but it is not twisty, and the interest is in the glimpses of the water and the parks. The best time to be here is in the evening in June, when the light stays low and golden until nearly midnight, or in September, when the parks turn yellow and the crowds thin. The wind from the gulf is cold even in July, and in winter the shore freezes and the roads are slippery.

Strelna, a town of nearly thirteen thousand people, has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, and Sosnovaya Polyana and Gorbunki, a little to the south-west, also have shops. A stop at the park is cheap and pleasant, and the coastal walk is a good way to rest. Those who want something more substantial can ride on to Peterhof, where the Grand Cascade and the Samson fountain are among the most visited sights in Russia. Rules for travel in Russia can change, so check them before you go.
t.the blocade ring@59.8,30.9:
The Blockade Ring stands on the south bank of the Neva, east of Saint Petersburg, close to where the Road of Life began its journey toward Lake Ladoga. It commemorates the siege of Leningrad, which lasted from September 1941 to January 1944, roughly 872 days, and the corridor that kept the city alive. When Shlisselburg fell in September 1941, the city was cut off by land, and the only lifeline ran across Ladoga, by boat in summer and over the ice in winter.

You come here along flat, open roads through marshy forest and birch, passing small settlements like Pavlovo, with Otradnoye as the nearest town of any size, about twenty thousand people and fuel stations. Kirovsk is a bit farther and larger. The terrain is a floodplain: low, wet, and thick with pine and alder, which made it hard to fight in and easy to understand why the front barely moved for years. The Nevsky Pyatachok bridgehead, a tiny strip of land held at terrible cost, lay on this stretch of river.

The riding is straightforward. Expect wide, fast roads shared with lorries, with the odd roadwork and frost heave, and long straights where wind from Ladoga can push a bike sideways. It is not a corner road, but a thoughtful one. Summer evenings are light well past ten, in June barely dark at all, and the mosquitoes in the wet woods are tireless. Winter is cold and grey, with the same low horizon that the defenders knew.

Memorials along the Road of Life are quiet, and many people leave flowers. In January 1943 the Soviet offensive broke the blockade, opening a narrow land corridor along the lake shore, and the full siege ended a year later. Take time here, and nearby at the Oreshek fortress in Shlisselburg, where the Neva leaves the lake. Bring respect: many visitors have family stories bound up with this ground.
t.ligovsky prospect@59.9,30.3:
Ligovsky Prospect is one of Saint Petersburg's long avenues, running south from Nevsky Prospect near Moscow Station, through old tenements, markets and railway yards toward the edge of the city. Its name comes from Ligovo, and the avenue follows the line of the old Ligovsky Canal, dug in the early eighteenth century under Peter the Great to bring water from the southern springs to the fountains of the Summer Garden. The canal has been covered or filled over most of its route, but the street still traces it, a straight line through the city's grid.

The avenue has many layers. Near the start are the old brick warehouses and the cafés of the railway district, while farther out, post-war housing and big factories take over. In the siege of Leningrad, from 1941 to 1944, the front line was only a few kilometres south of this district, and trams carried people to the factories under shellfire. Memorials, plaques and street names recall the war, and visitors often notice how many people still lay flowers.

Saint Petersburg is a city of five million, so fuel, food and workshops are everywhere, but riding in the centre is slow, with trams, cobbles and heavy traffic. Rails are slippery when wet, so cross them at a right angle. White Nights in June, when it hardly gets dark, are a special time, though the city is busy with visitors. Early morning, when the avenues are empty, is a lovely time to ride, with pale light on the stucco.

Outside the centre the roads open up. Highways to the south, such as the one toward Gostilitsy, run through flat, wooded country with a few villages, and summer weekends bring a rush of city dwellers heading to their dachas. Rain is frequent, and the weather can turn from sun to drizzle in minutes, so bring a jacket. Autumn turns the birches yellow, and winter is cold and dark, with ice and snow on the roads.
t.koltushskaya elevation@59.9,30.6:
East of Saint Petersburg, the land swells into a low ridge of moraine, left behind by the great ice sheet. The Koltushi Heights are not high, only some tens of metres above the surrounding plain, but in a country as flat as this, they are noticed. The landscape is a patchwork of pine and birch woods, wetland and open farmland, with the village of Koltushi scattered along the roads. A century ago it was a rural district, and the physiologist Ivan Pavlov, famous for his work on conditioned reflexes, founded a research station here, which people half-jokingly called the capital of conditioned reflexes.

During the Second World War, the ridge belonged to the ring of defences around Leningrad, and trenches, bunkers and batteries lie among the trees. The Northern battery No. 4, on the neighbouring ride, is part of the same system. Walking in these woods, you may still find shallow depressions and concrete remnants, so stay on paths and do not touch anything that looks like metal, because the region has unexploded ordnance.

Koltushi, with about ten thousand people, has fuel stations and supermarkets, and smaller places like Staraya and Yanino are close. Gatchina, a short way to the southwest, has a great palace built for Paul I, with an extensive park, and it makes a good pairing with this district. Local food is plain: pirozhki, soups and tea, with berries and mushrooms picked in the woods in late summer.

The Moskovskaya Road and the roads around Koltushi are flat to gently rolling, with fast traffic and plenty of trucks, but lanes through the villages are quieter. Rain is common, and the roads can be slippery after a shower. In June the evenings are bright until midnight, and the air is full of mosquitoes. In September, the mushroom season, the woods are busy with pickers, and in October the leaves are golden.
t.p k alexandrov s datcha@59.9,30.0:
Strelna lies at the beginning of the road to Peterhof, on the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, and its main feature is the Konstantinovsky Palace, begun in the reign of Peter the Great and named for a later grand duke, Konstantin. Like Peterhof, it was heavily damaged in the Second World War and later rebuilt, and in the early 2000s it was restored for the three-hundredth anniversary of Saint Petersburg. The park, with its canals and ponds, runs down toward the water, and the view across the gulf is wide and grey.

The dacha of P. K. Alexandrov is one of many wooden summer houses that line the streets around here, and I cannot say anything specific about its history. What can be said is that the district was a favourite summer retreat for Petersburgers from the nineteenth century, with villas, gardens and small ponds among the trees. The nearby forts, such as Seraya Loshad and Konstantin, stand out in the sea as part of the defences that once protected the capital from the Baltic, and they are visible on clear days.

Strelna, a town of nearly thirteen thousand people, has fuel, shops and cafés, and Gorbunki and Ol'gino are small places farther along the coast. Pushkin, with its Catherine Palace and the Amber Room, lies inland and makes a good partner for a day out. The Peterhof Highway is the main route, broad and fast, and it is lined with trees. Go early on a weekday to avoid the traffic jams that build on summer weekends.

For riders, the coast is flat and the roads are straightforward, with the pleasure lying in the light. In June the sun sets slowly and the sky stays pale blue and pink until after midnight, while in winter the gulf freezes at the edges and the sea haze is silver. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with fewer mosquitoes and fewer crowds, and the smell of the sea, a mix of salt, wet sand and reeds, drifts over the road.
t.historical centre of the town of pavlovs:
Pavlovsk was a gift. In 1777 Catherine the Great gave her son Paul, the future emperor, a stretch of forest and meadow south of Saint Petersburg, and he and his wife Maria Feodorovna turned it into one of the most elegant country residences in Russia. The Scottish architect Charles Cameron designed the palace, a pale yellow building with a shallow dome and a colonnade, and the park, which spreads over some six hundred hectares, was laid out in the English landscape manner, with winding paths, little bridges and pavilions half hidden among the trees. It is among the largest landscape parks in Europe, and walking in it on a quiet morning is a joy.

The town grew up around the estate, and its historical centre is a pleasant mix of wooden villas and old imperial buildings. In 1837 the first railway in Russia connected Tsarskoye Selo to Pavlovsk, and the station became a concert hall, called the Vauxhall after the London pleasure garden, where the young Johann Strauss II conducted summer seasons in the 1850s and 1860s. In the Second World War the palace was gutted during the German occupation, and the restoration took decades. The interiors now glow again with painted ceilings, gilded furniture and the great collection of Paul and Maria's treasures.

The country around is flat, wooded and marshy, laced with rivers and old canals, and the air smells of pine and wet moss. In autumn the park turns copper and gold, and the leaves float down on the ponds. In winter it is a snowy white landscape, and cross-country skiers use the avenues.

Riding here is easy but unexciting: broad, flat roads, a mixed surface and heavy traffic around Pushkin and the city. The park itself is a place for walking. Pavlovsk has fuel and shops, and Pushkin, about five kilometres away, is large, with plenty of cafés. Entry conditions for visitors can change, so check before you go. The best time is September, when the colours are rich, and the summer crowds have gone home.
t.soganli site@38.4,34.9:
Soğanlı lies in a side valley of Cappadocia that most tour buses skip, south-east of Ürgüp and Yeşilhisar, on the slopes of the volcanic uplands. The name means with onions, which tells you something about the humble character of the place. The valley sides are made of soft volcanic tuff, which the local Christians carved out in the Byzantine centuries into churches, chapels, monasteries, and houses. Many of the rock churches date from the ninth to the thirteenth century and keep fragments of frescoes: Karabaş, the Yılanlı or Snake church, the Barbara church and others, whose names reflect old stories more than documented history.

Unlike the better known valleys at Göreme, Soğanlı is quiet, spread over two arms of a small valley with scattered cones, cliffs and dovecotes. The pigeon houses, cut into the rock, were used to collect droppings for the vineyards and fields. The village has long been known for handmade cloth dolls, sold by local women under the trees near the entrance, and a walk up the valley, with the tuff glowing pink and grey in the afternoon light, is one of the pleasures of the area.

The roads to Soğanlı run through high, open country at around fifteen hundred metres, with the huge snowy cone of Mount Hasan, a dormant volcano, in the distance. The surface is generally good but the bends are a bit gentle and the traffic is light, mostly farm vehicles, dolmuş minibuses and the odd tour coach. Cold winds can come off the highlands, and winters are severe, with snow and frost, so it is best to visit from April to October. Summer afternoons are hot and dry, and early morning is the nicest time.

Derinkuyu, the underground city, is on the same ride, and the plateau between the two is a lovely, empty landscape of fields and low hills. Fuel is found in Yeşilhisar, Derinkuyu and Ürgüp, all towns of between twelve and seventeen thousand people, but not in the valley itself. Local restaurants in Ürgüp serve testi kebab, a stew cooked in a sealed clay pot and broken open at the table, which is the speciality of the region. Bring water and a hat for the walk, and expect a number of steep paths and stone steps.
t.church of panayia@35.0,32.8:
The Troodos mountains rise in the middle of Cyprus, covered in black pine, oak and cedar, with the summit of Mount Olympus at 1,952 metres, which gets snow in winter and has a small ski area. Hidden in the villages of the range are ten small churches that UNESCO listed in 2001, because their walls hold one of the finest collections of Byzantine and post-Byzantine wall paintings in the world, dating from the eleventh to the sixteenth centuries. The label does not say which church this is, and there are several dedicated to Panayia, the Virgin, so I will describe the group, which is what makes any one of them special.

From outside, these churches look plain, and the reason is practical. Most have a steep, tiled timber roof built over the original barrel-vaulted stone building, to shed the winter snow and rain, so the whole thing looks like a barn. Inside, the walls and ceilings are covered with frescoes: Christ in the dome, saints and prophets, scenes from the Gospels, and in some, lively donor portraits of the villagers who paid for the work. The colours, often deep blues, ochres and reds, glow in the dim light. Churches are small, some can be opened only by a key keeper, and there is often a request for a modest donation. Dress modestly and be quiet inside.

The mountain villages around, like Kakopetria with its old quarter of stone and timber houses, are a joy to visit, and the air is noticeably cooler than on the coast. Orchards of cherries, apples and walnuts, vineyards producing the sweet local wine, and shaded streams make a lovely setting. The food is plain and good: halloumi cheese, grilled meats, stewed lamb in clay pots, and honey.

The riding is among the best in the Mediterranean. The roads wind through the pine forests in long bends, with hairpins on the steeper sides and viewpoints over the valleys, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is light on weekdays, though weekends see more cars and coaches. Remember that in Cyprus traffic drives on the left. Snow and ice can affect the higher roads from December to March, and summers on the coast are very hot, so the mountains are a welcome escape.

Kakopetria and Kyperounta have small fuel stations, but the larger town of Lefka and the city of Nicosia offer the most choice. Spring, with wild flowers, and autumn are the best times.
t.the park alexandrova datchs@59.7,30.4:
Pavlovsk is among the largest landscape parks in Europe, and it began as a gift. In 1777 Catherine the Great gave the land to her son Paul, and he and his wife built a palace and a park here, which was designed by the Scottish architect Charles Cameron and then expanded over decades. The park covers more than five hundred hectares, and its mix of woods, meadows, rivers and pavilions is a model of the English landscape style adapted to the Russian plain.

The estate called Alexandrova Dacha belongs to the same world, one of the smaller properties that sprang up around the main palace as the imperial family grew. Pavlovsk's park is full of such corners, with winding paths, hidden temples, a pond with swans and avenues of old lime, birch and spruce. In autumn the colours are spectacular, and in winter the snow turns it into something close to a stage set.

Pavlovsk was also the end of Russia's first public railway, which opened in 1837 and ran from Saint Petersburg through Tsarskoye Selo to this spot. The station became a concert venue, and in the nineteenth century the Strauss family played here for crowds of holidaymakers who came out from the capital. That tradition of music in the park survives, with summer concerts held in and around the palace.

The ride south from the city is flat, but the roads of Pavlovsk and Tsarskoye Selo, lined with old trees, are pleasant. The main road from Saint Petersburg is busy, particularly on weekdays, and surfaces can be bumpy after winter, when frost heave breaks the tarmac. Quiet side roads near the park are lovely in the early morning, when the light is soft and the air smells of damp leaves.

Pavlovsk is a small town of sixteen thousand people with fuel, cafés and shops, and the park entrance is very close to the centre. Bring something warm, because even in summer the shade under the trees can be cool. Allow plenty of time, since the park is large and easy to get lost in.
t.yu p samoilova s villa@59.7,30.4:
Countess Yulia Samoilova is the sort of figure that the nineteenth century produced in numbers: rich, independent, beautiful, fond of artists and impatient with convention. She was a society woman who spent much of her life abroad, especially in Italy, and who is remembered in Russian painting as the muse of a famous artist. A villa on the southern edge of Saint Petersburg's estates bears her name, and it sits in the quiet country between Pavlovsk and Gatchina, in a landscape of old parks, small rivers and pine woods.

The label here also names the Prioratsky Park, which lies at Gatchina, a town with its own imperial history. The park is named for the Priory Palace, a curious building of local clay brick and stone that Emperor Paul I had made for the Knights of Malta, whose Grand Master he had become. The palace stands beside a lake in a wooded landscape, and it is one of those places where the mixture of ambition and eccentricity of the late eighteenth century is easy to feel.

Everything about this area suggests a world of country houses. The estates around Pavlovsk and Gatchina were places where the court escaped the formalities of the capital, and the buildings, parks and ponds that survive give a sense of the leisurely round of picnics, concerts and boat trips. Much was destroyed in the Second World War, and restoration has been a long job, with some buildings lovely and others still waiting.

Roads in this part of the Leningrad region run through flat farmland and forest, with long straights and occasional tight bends where a river is crossed. Surfaces can be rough after winter, with frost damage and patches. Traffic on the main roads to Pavlovsk and Gatchina is heavy during the day, so look for quieter lanes through the villages. The best time for riding is early morning in summer or on a clear autumn afternoon, when the birches turn gold.

Pavlovsk, four kilometres away, has pumps, cafés and shops, and there is a good choice of places to eat in Gatchina. Bring a rain jacket, since showers are frequent, and insect repellent if you plan to walk in the woods in summer.
t.church of panayia@35.0,33.0:
Cyprus has a church for every season, and the finest are hidden in the folds of the Troodos mountains. These small, plain stone chapels, with steep timber roofs that stretch over the older walls like a wide-brimmed hat to shed the winter snow, hide inside a world of colour: Byzantine frescoes, painted from the eleventh century to the sixteenth, of saints with huge dark eyes, scenes from the Gospels and the Virgin enthroned. A group of these painted churches in the Troodos region was listed as a World Heritage property in 1985. The Panayia, the Virgin, is the dedication of many of them, and the stop on this ride is among the foothills on the northern side of the range.

The frescoes were made by itinerant painters, some trained in Constantinople, others local, who worked on the walls with natural pigments and a lively sense of the human face. The painters often added portraits of donors, a monk, a knight or a family, kneeling at the feet of the saints. Light enters through narrow windows, and the interiors are dim and cool, with a smell of old wood, wax and stone, so wait for your eyes to adjust before looking up. The churches are often locked, and a caretaker keeps the key, so a small donation is appropriate, and photography may be restricted.

The Troodos range is a joy for riders, with smooth, well-surfaced roads that twist through pine forests and past terraced villages, with long views to the sea and a series of tight, well-engineered bends. Mount Olympus, at 1,952 metres, is the highest point on the island, and in winter it can be covered in snow, with a small ski area. Traffic on the island drives on the left, a legacy of the British period, and the roads are well signed in Greek and English. In summer, the mountains are cooler than the coast, and in spring, the wild flowers and almond blossom are lovely.

Lefka, thirteen kilometres by the map, is on the other side of the buffer zone, so for fuel the plain around Nicosia and the mountain villages on the southern side are the places to look, and it is wise to fill up before leaving the main roads. Local specialties include halloumi, the grilling cheese, honey, wine from the high villages and loukoumi, the soft sweet known elsewhere as Turkish delight. Carry water and a layer for the evening, since the mountains cool quickly after sunset.
t.serengeti national park@-2.7,34.9:
Siringet is the Maasai word for the endless plain, and the name was put on the maps by European visitors who heard it and wrote it down. The Serengeti is nearly fifteen thousand square kilometres of grassland, acacia woodland and granite outcrops called kopjes, in northern Tanzania, and each year more than a million wildebeest, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of zebra and gazelle, move through it in a great circular migration, following the rains and the new grass. In February they calve on the short-grass plains of the south, in May and June they head north-west toward the Grumeti river, and by July and August the herds reach the northern Mara river, where crocodiles wait at the crossings. The park, together with the neighbouring Ngorongoro Conservation Area, is listed as a World Heritage site.

I have to be straightforward about the riding. Motorcycles are not allowed in Tanzania's national parks, so you cannot ride into the Serengeti, and the visit is done in a four-wheel-drive vehicle with a guide and a pop-up roof. The ride belongs to the roads that lead up to it. From Arusha, the tarmac runs west through the farmland of the Rift Valley escarpment, past Lake Manyara and the town of Karatu, and up to the rim of Ngorongoro Crater at about 2,200 metres, where the road bends through cloud forest and the air is cool, damp and often foggy. The crater itself, a collapsed volcano, holds a self-contained world of lions, elephants and flamingos, and its rim road gives huge views.

Beyond the Ngorongoro gate, the road to the Serengeti runs past Olduvai Gorge, where the Leakey family found fossil remains of early humans, and the Maasai grazing lands, where herders in red cloaks guard cattle and goats. The roads are unpaved in places, with corrugations and dust, and should be treated as expedition travel, with the right vehicle and careful planning. Fuel is sold in Karatu and Arusha, and fuel inside the park is scarce, so check before you commit. The dry season, from June to October, is the best time for game viewing, and the green season, from November to May, brings rain, newborn animals and fewer visitors. Respect the animals and the Maasai, and never walk outside a vehicle in the park.
t.alexander palace and park@59.7,30.4:
Few Russian palaces have a story as heavy as the Alexander Palace in Pushkin, the town that grew around the imperial estate of Tsarskoye Selo, south of St Petersburg. Catherine the Great had it built for her grandson Alexander, the future Alexander I, by the Italian architect Giacomo Quarenghi in the 1790s, a restrained neoclassical building with a long colonnade facing the park. Its fame, though, comes from the last family to live in it. Nicholas II and his wife Alexandra preferred it to the grand Winter Palace, and they raised their five children here until the revolution of 1917, when the family was placed under house arrest in the palace before being sent east.

The Alexander Park around it is a landscape garden of ponds, shady paths and small follies, laid out in the English manner, and in autumn it is a good place for a walk, with the leaves turning and the light low. The much larger Catherine Palace, a short way off, is the better-known attraction, with its blue and gold façade and the reconstructed Amber Room, whose original panels disappeared in the Second World War. The town was renamed after the poet Pushkin, who studied at the Lyceum here as a boy, and the school building still stands beside the Catherine Palace.

The ride in from St Petersburg is an easy run of about twenty-five kilometres south, mostly on busy urban roads and highways, so it is not a place for twisting bends. What you enjoy is the flatness and the northern light, which in June and early July, during the white nights, lasts almost until dawn. Expect heavy traffic on the main roads on weekends, wet cobbles in town after rain and short riding seasons: the weather is reliable only from May to September.

Pushkin has about ninety thousand inhabitants, so fuel stations, cafés and shops are plentiful. Parking near the palaces can be crowded, and a bike is easier to place than a car. Check the opening hours and the ticket arrangements for the palace before you set out, since visiting rules have changed from time to time, and bring a rain jacket whatever the forecast says.
t.historical centre of the village of stre:
Strelna is where Peter the Great first looked at the Gulf of Finland from the south shore and decided that his new capital needed a country palace worthy of Versailles. He began a residence here in the early eighteenth century, before settling on Peterhof, a few kilometres to the west, and the estate was later developed by his daughter Elizabeth and then given to the Grand Duke Konstantin, whose name it still bears in the Konstantinovsky Palace. In the 2000s the palace was restored and today it is used for state receptions and conferences, with the grounds open to visitors on a part-time basis. The historic centre of the village is a small area of old streets near the shore.

Between the palace and the water lies a park with canals and ponds, and the Gulf of Finland, shallow and brackish, stretches to the horizon. In winter it freezes, and fishermen walk on the ice. The shoreline here is flat and reedy, a sharp contrast to the rocky coasts of the Finnish side, and birdwatchers come in spring and autumn to see migrating ducks, geese and waders.

For a rider, the main road is the Peterhof Highway, a wide and fast route that runs along the south shore from St Petersburg to Peterhof and beyond. It is scenic in the sense that it passes palaces and parks rather than bends. The surface is generally good, but traffic is dense in the morning and evening rush hours, and in summer the weekend crush toward Peterhof's fountains can slow it to a crawl. Early morning is the best time, and the white nights give you light until late.

Strelna has about twelve thousand people, so fuel and food are available in the village, and the larger town of Sosnovaya Polyana lies a few kilometres inland. A coffee in a café near the palace gate is a good way to enjoy the quiet before the day-trippers arrive. In winter the road can be icy and wet, and the riding season is short, so plan for May to September and take a warm layer even then, since the wind off the Gulf can be cold.
t.tupelo@34.3,-88.7:
Tupelo is where the Natchez Trace Parkway keeps its headquarters, and it is a fitting place to begin or end a day on that road. The Trace itself is older than any highway in the country, a path worn into the earth by bison, then by the Chickasaw and Choctaw, then by boatmen who floated cargo down the Mississippi to Natchez and walked home through the woods. The modern parkway follows that line for 444 miles to Nashville, a ribbon of smooth asphalt with no trucks, no billboards, no traffic lights and a speed limit of 50 miles an hour that rangers take seriously.

Tupelo, a city of about thirty-five thousand, has two claims to fame. One is that Elvis Presley was born here in 1935 in a two-room house that you can still visit, along with the church where he first sang gospel and a hardware store where his mother is said to have bought his first guitar. The other is that it was the first city to take electricity from the Tennessee Valley Authority, in 1934, a fact that has made it quietly proud ever since. The Civil War also left its mark, with the Battle of Tupelo in July 1864 marked by a small park and monuments on the edge of town.

The ride is the point of the exercise. North from here the parkway runs through rolling hardwood forest and across old fields, over cypress swamps and low ridges, and the corners are gentle, long and perfectly banked. There is almost nothing to do but ease along at the limit and watch the light shift through the trees. Deer, wild turkeys and the odd armadillo wander near the road, and in spring dogwoods and redbuds line the verges. Autumn brings a quieter beauty, with sweet gum and hickory turning the woods copper, and the roads are nearly empty.

Practical things are easy in Tupelo and hard on the Trace. The city has fuel, food and hotels in abundance, but the parkway has no commercial services, so top up the tank and the stomach before you leave. Plantersville and Verona, a few kilometres away, are small places that have small-town cafés. The Trace has picnic areas and restrooms at intervals, and the visitor centre outside town is worth an hour, with maps, a film and friendly rangers.
t.french camp@33.3,-89.4:
French Camp is a tiny settlement on the Natchez Trace Parkway in central Mississippi, and it holds more history than its size suggests. In the early nineteenth century, a French-Canadian named Louis LeFleur established a stand here, a place where travellers on the old Trace could find a meal and a bed, and the community took its name from him. The site lay in Choctaw country, and LeFleur's family had Choctaw connections, which made the place a meeting point between peoples. Later, in 1822, a school was founded at French Camp, and it grew into a boarding academy that still operates today.

The little cluster of buildings beside the Parkway has a rewarding, off-the-record feel. A pair of log cabins, one of them dating from the early nineteenth century, stand under big trees, with a restored house nearby, and a small museum tells the story of the Trace and the people who used it. Sorghum syrup and cornbread are the local traditions, and a good number of Parkway travellers stop for just that. In warm weather the shade and the sound of cicadas are very agreeable.

Riding the Trace through this part of Mississippi is quiet and dreamlike. The road runs along ridges and through wooded valleys, with long straight sections and gentle bends, past old cotton fields that have gone back to pine and hardwood. The speed limit is low, the surface is mostly smooth and the traffic is thin, so you can relax and look around. Wildlife is plentiful, with deer, wild turkeys and the occasional armadillo trundling along the verge. Heat and humidity in summer can be intense, and thunderstorms arrive with little warning.

Fuel is not available on the Parkway, so you need to leave it to fill up. Kosciusko, a town of about seven thousand people about thirty kilometres to the south, is the nearest place with stations, restaurants and motels, and it is also the birthplace of Oprah Winfrey. Winona and Durant are options farther north and south. Bring water and a snack, and be aware that many facilities along the Trace keep short hours and are closed on some days. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with comfortable temperatures and bright, clear light.
t.gods window@-24.9,30.9:
God's Window is a viewpoint at the edge of the Drakensberg escarpment in Mpumalanga, and the name tells you what to expect. The cliff falls away almost a kilometre to the Lowveld below, a flat, hazy plain of bush and farmland that stretches east toward Kruger National Park and the Mozambique border. On a clear morning you can see an astonishing distance, and on a misty one the whole plain vanishes under cloud and you are left standing on the roof of a white sea. Weather is capricious here, and even in summer a fog can swallow the view within minutes, so give yourself a margin.

A short path climbs through a pocket of rainforest to the top of a rocky outcrop, with a good view of the mountain wall running north and south. The escarpment catches moisture from the Indian Ocean, and the slopes are covered in lush forest, tree ferns and wild flowers. Nearby is the old gold-mining village of Pilgrim's Rest, where a rush in the 1870s drew thousands of prospectors and the town is now a living museum, and Graskop, a small town with craft shops and pancake houses.

The Panorama Route follows the lip of the escarpment on the R532, a smooth, scenic road with broad bends and short climbs. Traffic includes tour buses and trucks, particularly in the middle of the day, so rise early for clear views and light traffic. Mist and rain are possible at any time, and the road can be slippery. Winter days, from May to September, are dry and cool, with the clearest air, while summer brings afternoon thunderstorms and warm, humid mornings.

Fuel is available in Graskop, the nearest sizeable town, and in Hazyview and Sabie, and you should fill up before setting out along the route. A small entrance fee is charged at the viewpoint, and local traders sell crafts in the car park. Keep a close eye on your bike, since opportunist theft happens at tourist car parks.
t.bourkes luck potholes@-24.7,30.8:
Where the Treur River meets the Blyde, the water has carved a set of smooth, round potholes into the rock, some of them deep enough to swallow a car, and the effect is a little like looking into the inside of a giant's pocket. The potholes are cylindrical bowls of yellow, orange and grey dolomite, created over thousands of years by whirlpools spinning sand and pebbles against the riverbed. A series of footbridges and paths lets visitors look down into them from above, with the river rushing through the channels below.

The names tell a story. Treur means mourning in Afrikaans, and Blyde means joyful. In the 1840s, Voortrekker families travelling through the area left their wives behind while the men went to scout. When the men failed to return, the women named the first river mourning, but the men came back safely and the river where they were reunited was named joyful. The potholes themselves are named for Tom Bourke, a prospector who staked a claim here in the nineteenth century and was sure there was gold in the river bed. He found little, and his luck proved to be mostly a name.

For the rider, this is a short stop on the Panorama Route, the road linking the great viewpoints of the Blyde River Canyon, one of the largest green canyons in the world. The surface is generally good, the bends gentle, and the scenery is a mix of forest, grassland and rock. Rain can come quickly in summer afternoons, and the footbridges become slippery, so go carefully in wet weather. The morning light is best, with fewer crowds and a cooler, clearer atmosphere.

There is an entrance fee at the gate, paid on the spot, and a small café and a craft market are on site. Fuel is not available at the potholes, so fill up in Graskop or Hoedspruit before you set out. Wear shoes with decent grip and keep to the paths, because the rock can be treacherous. Allow an hour, and take time at the lower bridge, where the river leaves the potholes and tumbles into the canyon.
t.three rondavels@-24.6,30.8:
Three huge, round-topped pillars of rock stand along the rim of the Blyde River Canyon, and local people liken them to the rondavels, the round thatched huts of traditional African homesteads, which is how they got their name. Each is a dome of dark rock, capped with grass and bush, rising hundreds of metres above the water. Local tradition links them to the wives of a chief, and the place is treated with some respect.

Below the viewpoint, the canyon plunges several hundred metres to the Blyde River Dam, where green water fills the bottom of the gorge. The canyon is about twenty-five kilometres long, and often described as one of the largest green canyons in the world, because the slopes are clothed in lush vegetation instead of bare rock. Baboons and vervet monkeys visit the car park, so keep food out of sight, and eagles ride the thermals along the cliff. In the early morning, when mist fills the gorge, the pillars rise like islands from a white sea.

The ride out to the viewpoint is the end of the Panorama Route, along a smooth tarmac road between farmland and forest. It is a quiet, flowing road, though a little narrow in places, with trucks carrying timber from the plantations. Rain can set in without warning in the summer months, and in winter the dawn can be cold. The best time is early morning, when the colours are strongest and the crowds are small.

There are no services at the viewpoint apart from a few craft sellers and a small kiosk, so plan ahead. Fuel is available in Graskop, about thirty kilometres away, and in Hoedspruit to the north. A small entrance fee may apply at the gate. Take water, keep your helmet and jacket close and spend a few quiet minutes at the railing, because the view is worth the long ride.
t.derinkuyu@38.4,34.7:
Beneath the ordinary Anatolian town of Derinkuyu lies a city. It was dug into the soft volcanic rock, tuff, that underlies the Cappadocia plateau, and it descends through many levels, with stables, kitchens, wine presses, storerooms, chapels and living quarters, all linked by narrow tunnels and stairways. Only the upper levels are open to visitors, but even these give a powerful sense of how large and organised the place was, and the air grows cooler and heavier as you go down.

Nobody knows exactly when it was begun, but the city seems to have been expanded over centuries, and it is often linked with the Byzantine period, when local Christians used underground refuges during raids and wars. The designers were ingenious: ventilation shafts bring fresh air from the surface, a well supplies water, and round stone doors, like millstones, could be rolled across passages from the inside to block intruders. The doors are still there, and you can see the grooves in which they ran. The city could shelter thousands of people along with animals and food stores for long periods.

The modern find is a story told with relish locally: in the 1960s, a man knocked down a wall in his house and found a hidden room, which led to a tunnel and eventually to the whole complex. The landscape above gives no hint. The town is a modest market place of low houses, shops and a mosque, and the surrounding plateau is flat farmland with fields of potatoes and orchards. That ordinary surface makes the subterranean world even more surprising.

The ride here from Nevşehir crosses open, rolling land, with strange cones and rock formations rising in the distance, and the roads are mostly good, wide and quiet. Dry, bright weather is the norm, and the best months are spring and autumn, when the days are warm and the evenings cool; midsummer is hot, and winter can be cold and snowy. Wind across the plateau can be strong, and farm vehicles use the roads, so keep an eye out.

Tunnels are narrow and low, so the visit involves stooping, and crowds can be tight at midday, which makes early morning the best time to go. Derinkuyu is a real town of over twelve thousand people, with fuel stations, cafés and shops, and it is a sensible place to fill up and eat. Simple restaurants serve grilled meat, lentil soup, flatbread and sweet tea, and pottery stalls sell local ceramics.

Bring a light jacket, since the temperature below ground stays cool, and take your time.
t.uchisar@38.6,34.8:
Everyone in Cappadocia ends up looking at Uçhisar, because it is the tallest thing for miles. A great knuckle of volcanic rock rises out of the village, honeycombed with windows and doorways, and for centuries it served as a citadel, the name itself meaning something like the fortress at the end. Climb the stairs inside and you step out onto the top with the whole plateau spread beneath you: valleys of pale tuff, pinnacles, vineyards, orchards, and far off on a clear day the snowy cone of Erciyes, a dormant volcano near Kayseri.

The rock is the story. Eruptions from ancient volcanoes laid down thick layers of ash that hardened into soft tuff, and wind and water have since carved it into the chimneys and cones that make this region look like a stage set. Because tuff is easy to cut and hardens on exposure, people have been digging homes, churches, storerooms and pigeon lofts into it for thousands of years. Look at the cliff faces around Uçhisar and you will see small square openings, often painted or carved, which were pigeon houses; the birds were valued for their droppings, which fertilised the vineyards.

The ride is short and gentle. From Göreme the road climbs in easy bends to the village, with good asphalt and light traffic outside the busy months, though tour buses and quad bikes crowd the lanes near the viewpoints at sunset. Wind can be strong on the exposed ridge, and the cobbled lanes inside the village are slippery when wet or dusty, so park on the edge and walk. Early morning is magical, when hot-air balloons rise from the valleys and drift past the rock in silence, their burners flaring now and then.

Practical matters are straightforward. Uçhisar is small, but Göreme, three kilometres away, and Nevşehir, about eight, have petrol stations, shops and plenty of restaurants. In the village there are cafés with terraces facing the rock, serving strong Turkish coffee, tea and sweet pastries, and a glass of local wine from nearby vineyards is easy to find in the evening. In winter the plateau can be bitterly cold and snowy, with the cones dusted white, which is a quiet and beautiful time to see it.

Bring a layer for the top, because the wind is cooler than you expect, and allow an hour to climb and look.
t.goreme@38.6,34.8:
Göreme is the village at the centre of the postcard. Around it, in the valleys and ridges of the Cappadocia plateau, stand the fairy chimneys, tall cones of pale tuff capped with harder rock, and every other cliff face is pierced with windows and doors. The place has the odd, dreamlike quality of a landscape shaped by ash, water and patient hands, and people have lived inside it for as long as anyone can say.

The cleverest thing about it is what the Christians made there. From the early centuries of the Byzantine period, monks and villagers carved churches, chapels and monasteries into the rock, and the Göreme Open Air Museum, a short walk from the village, preserves a cluster of them. Inside, painted ceilings and walls show saints and scenes from the Gospels in reds, ochres and blues, some of them worn, some astonishingly fresh. Two of the churches are famous for their frescoes, and a dark one retains vivid colour because little daylight reached it. Together with the surrounding area, the site has been listed by UNESCO since the 1980s. Opening hours and ticketing are managed, so check before you go.

The ride around Göreme is a pleasure. Roads wind between cones and fields on good surfaces, quiet outside midday, and every turn brings a new shape. Sunrise is the time to be on the move, with dozens of balloons filling the sky above the valleys, and sunset turns the tuff pink and gold. Wind can pick up in the afternoons, and tour buses and quad bikes can clog the lanes in season, so give yourself time. In winter the weather is cold, with occasional snow, and the landscape takes on a hush.

The village itself is touristy but charming, with cave hotels built into the rock, cafés with carpeted terraces, and restaurants serving testi kebab, a stew cooked in a sealed clay pot that the waiter breaks open at the table. Pottery, carpets and lamps fill the shops. Fuel is easiest in Nevşehir or Ürgüp, each a short ride away, as Göreme itself has limited options. Car parks fill early, but motorcycles can generally squeeze in.

Take time to walk one of the valleys, such as Rose or Love Valley, where the rock changes colour with the light. The scale is human and the calm unexpected.
t.avanos@38.7,34.8:
Avanos is a pottery town on the Kızılırmak, the Red River, which is the longest river in Turkey and which cuts across the Cappadocia plateau on its way to the Black Sea. The river takes its name from the colour of the clay it carries, and the clay is why the town exists. For thousands of years potters here have dug the red earth from the banks, shaped it on kick wheels and fired it in kilns, a craft that is said to go back to Hittite times and still shapes the main street today.
