You can watch it happen. Workshops open onto the street, where craftsmen sit at low wheels, spinning jugs, plates and the big lidded pots used for cooking, and many will let visitors try. Shelves of ceramics in red, brown and bright glazes crowd the shops, and the quality ranges from tourist souvenirs to serious pieces. The town also has a strange attraction in a pottery shop whose cave walls are covered in locks of hair left by women who visited over the decades, a curiosity that has become famous in its own right.

The river gives the place a different mood from the dry plateau. Willows and poplars grow along its banks, a stone bridge crosses it, and in the evening people sit by the water and drink tea. The road between Göreme and Avanos runs over rolling land with views of pinnacles and cliffs, and it is an easy ride on mostly good asphalt, with some patched sections and farm traffic. In summer the afternoons are hot and bright, so mornings and evenings are better, and in winter the days are cold, with frost and occasional snow.

Avanos is a real town, with nearly thirteen thousand people, shops, bakeries and petrol stations, so it is a handy place to fill the tank, buy water and find lunch. Grilled meat, lentil soup, gözleme, a thin filled flatbread, and Turkish tea fit the setting, and the bakeries sell fresh simit, a sesame-coated bread ring. Parking is easy near the river, and pottery can be shipped if you cannot carry it.

Sit by the water for a while. The river, unlike the rock formations, is a quiet thing, and it has been shaping life here for a very long time.
t.urgup@38.6,34.9:
Ürgüp has the air of a town that is comfortable with itself. It is one of the larger places on the Cappadocia plateau, with some sixteen thousand people, and it spreads across the foot of a rocky hill pocked with old cave dwellings, with stone houses in the old quarter and a lively centre of shops and cafés. Unlike Göreme, it has not been wholly given over to visitors, and in the evening the main square fills with families and teenagers rather than tour groups.

The stone houses are a delight. Many were built by Greek and Armenian craftsmen in the nineteenth century, using the same pale tuff that surrounds the town, with arched doorways and carved window frames, and some have been turned into boutique hotels. Rock-cut churches and dwellings lie in the cliffs above, and a hill at the edge of town gives a view across rooftops to the strange cones beyond. The region has an ancient tradition of winemaking, thanks to the volcanic soil and dry climate, and the vineyards around Ürgüp produce local grapes with names that few people outside Turkey know. Many small wineries welcome visitors, and tasting the local red is a pleasure, though a sip is wise if you are riding.

The roads around Ürgüp are among the best on the plateau, with wide, smooth asphalt winding between fields and rock formations, and gentle gradients, so riding is relaxed. Traffic is light outside the high season, though minibuses and tractors share the road. In summer the sun is intense, and the plateau can be hot and dusty, so start early. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear light, cool mornings and colourful fields. Winter brings cold, sometimes snow, which makes the cones look strange and beautiful.

Practically, Ürgüp is the sensible base on the plateau. It has petrol stations, banks, pharmacies, supermarkets and a good choice of restaurants, so you can fill the tank and restock easily. Local dishes include manti, small dumplings with yoghurt, pottery kebab cooked in clay, and sweet dishes with walnuts and grape molasses. The market is lively on the weekly market day, with fruit, vegetables, cheese and textiles piled on tables.

An evening stroll through the old streets, with the smell of grilled meat and the sound of conversation, is worth the time.
t.vasilyevo@57.0,34.9:
Vasilyevo is a name that appears on the map of the Tver countryside many times over, and it is better treated as a way into the landscape than as a destination in itself. This one lies a few kilometres from Torzhok, on the old route between Tver and the north-west, in a land of low hills, wide fields and slow rivers, with the Tvertsa flowing through it on its way to the Volga. The villages are small, the churches are often half-ruined, and the sense of space is considerable.

Torzhok is the real attraction. It is one of the oldest towns in the region, founded as a trading post on the border of Novgorod's territory, and it grew rich on the grain that was sent along the river to the north. Its churches and monasteries line the banks of the Tvertsa, and the Boris and Gleb Monastery has a collection of old towers and cathedrals. The town is famous for gold embroidery, a craft in which women stitched patterns of thread onto velvet and leather, and for a dish of minced chicken cutlets that was supposedly invented at an inn here and made famous by Pushkin, who passed through on his journeys between Moscow and St Petersburg. The writer's name is attached to several corners of the town.

For riding, the approach is the old highway, the M10, which carries heavy traffic between Moscow and St Petersburg, and the better experience is on the smaller roads that run alongside it and through the villages. Surfaces vary a lot, from smooth new asphalt to rough, broken patches, and the lorries on the main road are a reminder to stay alert. In the evening, the light on the river and the fields is soft, and the birch woods glow in the late sun.

Torzhok is six kilometres away and has everything a rider needs, with a population of nearly fifty thousand, plenty of fuel, a good choice of cafes and a historic centre worth a walk. Villages on this stretch have little in the way of services, so use the town for supplies. Late spring and early autumn are the pleasantest seasons, when the roads are drier and the mosquitoes are fewer, and in winter the road can be icy and the days are short.
t.iversky monastery@58.0,33.3:
Most monasteries are built on hills; this one is on an island. The Iversky Monastery stands on Selvitsky Island in Lake Valdai, a few kilometres from the town of Valday, and the sight of its white walls and gilded domes across the water is one of the great images of the Russian north-west. Patriarch Nikon founded it in 1653, copying the Iviron Monastery on Mount Athos, and the same ambition that created New Jerusalem is visible here, in the conviction that the Russian landscape could host a holy place as grand as any in the East.

The country around it is the Valdai Hills, the highest ground in the region, though that is not saying much, with the summits barely reaching three hundred metres. What makes them important is the water: the Volga, the Dnieper and the Western Dvina all rise in the district, and the many lakes, among them Valdai itself, are the legacy of glaciers. The land is thick with spruce, birch and aspen, and much of it is protected as a national park. The air is clean and cold, the lakes are clear, and in autumn the forest goes through every shade of red and gold.

Valday has another claim to fame: bells. When Ivan the Great crushed Novgorod in 1478 and carried off its veche bell, the symbol of the city's freedom, the bell was sent into exile in Valdai, and the town became a centre of bell founding. Valdai bells, small and clear, were once hung on the harnesses of post-horses, and they have been made here ever since. There is a museum of them in the town.

The road from Valday to the monastery is short and easy, and the highway that serves the area, the old Moscow to St Petersburg route, passes nearby, so traffic can be heavy with lorries. The side roads that wind between the lakes are far quieter and have a comfortable, rolling character, with decent surfaces and long views across the water. Valday has fuel, shops and cafes, and a population of about eighteen thousand. Boats cross to the island in the warmer months, so check before you plan. Early autumn is the time to come, when the forest is alight and the lake is calm.
t.ruins of leon viejo@12.4,-86.6:
Hernandez de Cordoba founded the first city of Leon in 1524 on the shore of Lake Managua, and what remains of it are the foundations of a Spanish colonial town sunk in a dry, hot plain under the cone of Momotombo. The volcano is the great feature of the landscape, a near-perfect cone that rises across the water and sometimes sends up a plume of steam. Its eruptions and a series of earthquakes made the site dangerous, and in 1610 the inhabitants abandoned it and rebuilt the city further west, where Leon stands now. Archaeologists excavated the old town from the 1960s, and the ruins of the plaza, the cathedral, the convents and the governor's house now lie in neat rows of low stone walls.

Hernandez de Cordoba was executed here in 1526 on the orders of Pedrarias Davila, the governor, who had come to suspect him of disloyalty. The story is one of the grim episodes of the Spanish conquest, and Pedrarias ruled the province harshly until his death in 1531, and the ruins are a place to think about what Spanish rule meant for the people who lived here.

The ride from Managua is straightforward. The highway to Leon runs northwest across a flat, dusty plain, and the turn to the ruins is just beyond La Paz Centro, a town of potters known for its clay oven-fired ceramics and its quesillo, a soft cheese wrapped in a tortilla. The last stretch is on a smaller road through fields, and the surface can be rough. Traffic is a mix of trucks, buses, horse-drawn carts and bicycles, and speed limits are loosely observed. Heat is intense, particularly from March to May, and afternoon storms arrive in the wet season.

Fuel is available in La Paz Centro and Nagarote, about nine and sixteen kilometres away, and food is simple and cheap: gallo pinto, grilled meat, fresh tortillas and fruit juices. The site has a small museum and visitors can walk among the ruins in an hour. Bring water and a hat, as shade is scarce. The best time is the dry season, from December to April, and the light is lovely in the late afternoon.
t.zuma@18.4,31.7:
Zuma lies on the Nile in northern Sudan, near the town of Merowe, close to the Fourth Cataract, and its tombs are a reminder that this was once the heartland of a Nubian empire. From about the eighth century BC the kings of Kush, based at Napata, ruled both their own country and Egypt, as the 25th Dynasty, and later retreated south and built their capital at Meroe. When they died, the kings of Napata were buried under pyramids. At El-Zuma, a group of royal tombs, mounds and pyramids lies in the desert on the west bank, and nearby Nuri holds the greater pyramids of the kings. Nearby Nuri and Jebel Barkal are part of a UNESCO listing of the Napatan region, made in 2003.

The desert here is stark and beautiful, a plain of pale sand and dark rock under a huge sky. The Nile cuts through it in a green band of date palms, fields and mud-brick villages, and the contrast between the water and the dunes is startling. Heat is intense through most of the year, and the wind blows sand across the roads. From November to February the temperatures are bearable, with cool mornings, and that is the season for travel.

Be honest about the present: Sudan has been in the grip of armed conflict since April 2023, and travel in much of the country is dangerous and often impossible. Foreign governments advise against travel, and anyone dreaming of this route should check up-to-date information and wait for the situation to improve. In better times, the road along the Nile from Khartoum to Merowe, on a modern highway, was a quiet, fast run through the desert, with a few sharp bends and some checkpoints.

Merowe, thirteen kilometres away, is a town of ten thousand people, with fuel and a market, and has grown since the building of the Merowe Dam, which created a long lake upstream and displaced local communities. Kuraymah, on the opposite side, is larger. In normal times, tea sellers and food stalls along the road offered fried fish, lentils and flat bread, and the people were famous for their hospitality to strangers.
t.nuri@18.6,31.9:
Nuri is where the kings of Napata are buried, in a desert cemetery on the west bank of the Nile, a little downstream of Jebel Barkal, and it holds the largest group of royal pyramids in Sudan. The first, and largest, belongs to Taharqa, the Kushite pharaoh who ruled Egypt and Nubia in the seventh century BC, and who is mentioned in the Bible as a king who came out against the Assyrians. His pyramid once rose around fifty metres high, in steep, narrow form that is typical of Nubian examples, and it contained a burial chamber cut deep into the rock and reached by a stair. Around it, the pyramids of more than twenty kings and many queens stand in rows, many of them partly collapsed.

Nubian pyramids differ from Egyptian ones. They are smaller, steeper, built of sandstone blocks with a rubble core, and each stood in front of a chapel for offerings. Most were looted in antiquity, and a large number of the finds were removed by archaeologists in the early twentieth century, including funerary statues, which are now in museums in Khartoum and Boston. The cemetery at Nuri was excavated by an American team around 1916, and the statues of Taharqa and his successors can be seen in museum halls.

The country here is dry, hot and spare. A strip of irrigated land, a few kilometres wide, runs along the river, and beyond it lies the Bayuda or Libyan desert, with dark hills in the distance. Date palms, sorghum fields and small villages dot the bank, and the people are Nubian, with their own languages and a deep pride in the ancient heritage. The road along the Nile is quiet. The best season is from November to February, when the days are warm and mornings cool.

The situation in Sudan today is very serious. A war that began in April 2023 has caused immense suffering and made most travel impossible. Foreign ministries advise against any journey, and it would be unwise to plan a visit until peace returns. The pyramids have stood for twenty-seven centuries and will wait.

Kuraymah, seven kilometres from Nuri, is a town of almost twenty thousand people with fuel and food, and Merowe, a short distance further, has more. Bring water and a hat if you ever come.
t.gordion@39.6,32.0:
King Midas is the name everyone remembers, and this mound of earth near the village of Yassıhöyük is where his world really sat. Gordion was the capital of the Phrygians, a people who ruled much of central Anatolia in the centuries after the Hittite collapse, and the ruins lie on the flat floodplain of the Sakarya river, west of Ankara and about fifteen kilometres from Polatlı.

The riding here is honest plateau riding. You leave the capital on fast, wide roads through wheat and barley country, and the landscape flattens into a huge pale bowl with a few poplar lines and the odd grain silo for punctuation. Corners are rare and gentle. What you get instead is space, a big sky and a steady crosswind in the afternoon, so a good mid-morning start in spring or early summer is kinder than a July noon, when the steppe bakes and the tarmac shimmers. In late autumn the fields are bare brown and the light turns long and golden, which suits the place.

The great tumulus is the thing to see first. It rises like a small hill beside the road, and under it lies a wooden tomb chamber of cedar and juniper that is generally described as the oldest standing timber building in the world, dating from around the eighth century BC. You walk in through a tunnel cut into the mound, which is a strange, cool, quiet experience after the glare outside. The museum next door holds the finds, including delicate inlaid wooden furniture and bronze vessels that were buried with the dead for a funeral feast.

Then there is the knot. Gordion is the town where, in 333 BC, Alexander the Great is said to have been shown the tangled cart of King Gordius and to have solved the puzzle with a stroke of his sword, whatever the details of that story really were. It is a good tale to have in your head while you stand on the citadel mound looking at the gate and the old walls.

Practical matters are simple. There is nothing at the site beyond the visitor facilities, so fill the tank in Polatlı, which is a proper town of tens of thousands with fuel stations, bakeries and tea houses on the way. Bring water and a hat, because shade on the mound is scarce, and give yourself an hour or two. Morning is best, before the wind picks up and the tour coaches arrive from Ankara.
t.neolithic site of catalhoyuk@37.7,32.8:
Nine thousand years ago, people here lived in a town with no streets. Çatalhöyük is a pair of low mounds on the Konya plain, and what makes it famous is how its houses were packed together wall to wall, entered by ladders through the roof, with the dead buried under the floors and bulls' horns plastered into the walls. It is one of the earliest large settlements anywhere and has been a World Heritage site since 2012.

Getting there from Konya is easy and very flat. You head south-east on straight roads through irrigated fields and sugar beet, with the town of Çumra eleven kilometres away, and the Taurus mountains standing as a faint blue wall on the horizon. This is the great Anatolian steppe, where the sky does most of the work. There is little to challenge a rider except wind and the occasional tractor, so it is a day for relaxed cruising rather than corners. Spring is lovely, when the plain is green and the far mountains still carry snow, whereas high summer is dry, dusty and hot by midday.

The site itself is more understated than people expect. There is no pile of monumental stone, because everything was built of mud brick, so you walk on raised walkways above the excavations while a large protective roof shades the digging area. A reconstructed house helps you picture the thing: a single room, a hearth, platforms for sleeping, painted plaster. The finds, among them the seated figurines of heavy-hipped women, are mostly in the museums in Konya and Ankara, but the setting explains why a settled farming community chose this place, with the ancient wetlands and fertile alluvium of the old Çarşamba river delta.

A few things are worth knowing. The little town beside the mound is small, and Çumra is the better choice for fuel, a hot meal and a cold drink. Konya itself, with its whirling-dervish heritage and its fine Seljuk buildings, is the natural place to eat in the evening, and the local speciality of slow-baked mutton, etli ekmek, a long thin meat flatbread, is worth hunting down.

Give it an hour or so, wear a hat, and carry water, since shade is rare. The reward is the odd sensation of standing on the spot where something very close to our own way of life, with its houses, its neighbours and its ancestors in the floor, began to take shape.
t.graskop@-24.9,30.8:
Graskop perches right on the lip of the Drakensberg escarpment in Mpumalanga, where the highveld plateau drops about a thousand metres to the lowveld below, and nearly everything worth seeing in the area is a view. It is a small tourist town with craft stalls, cafes and guesthouses, and its position at the top of the Panorama Route makes it the natural base. Locals call the edge here the Berg, and when the mist comes up from the lowveld in the morning it fills the gaps between the forested spurs like milk.

The sights are strung along the road within a short ride. God's Window looks out over the lowveld on a clear day all the way to the Kruger Park, and nearby are the Pinnacle, a single quartzite spire rising from the forest, and Lisbon Falls and Berlin Falls, which pour over the lip of the plateau. Further north, the Blyde River Canyon cuts into the escarpment for about twenty kilometres, one of the largest green canyons in the world, with the Three Rondavels, huge round rock formations, rising above the Blyde dam. The name of the river, which means river of joy, was given by Voortrekkers who returned safely after leaving their party on the river Treur, the river of sorrow.

Gold built the region. In the 1870s prospectors found alluvial gold nearby, and Pilgrim's Rest, a few kilometres to the northeast, became a boom town, now preserved as a living museum with tin-roofed Victorian houses. The pine and eucalyptus plantations that cover many of the hills were planted to supply the mines with timber, and they give the air its resinous smell.

The riding is rewarding but needs care. Roads on and below the escarpment are generally paved, with smooth bends, hairpins on the descents and long views. Mist and heavy rain are common, particularly in summer from November to March, and the road can be slick, while fog can shut out the view entirely. Potholes appear after the rains, and minibus taxis, trucks and pedestrians share the road, so ride defensively. Winter, from May to August, is dry and clear, with cold mornings.

Graskop has fuel stations, a few supermarkets and a good number of places to eat, with the small town's cafes famous for stuffed pancakes. Beyond, towns are spaced out, so fill the tank here before heading up the Panorama Route. Keep valuables out of sight at viewpoints, where opportunistic theft has been reported, and enjoy the cool air at the top.
t.veliky novgorod@58.5,31.3:
Veliky Novgorod calls itself Russia's oldest city, with a chronicle date of 859, and for several centuries it was one of the most important cities in the country. It sits on the Volkhov river just north of Lake Ilmen, on the trade route between the Baltic and Byzantium, and in the Middle Ages it governed a huge territory in the north. Unusually for medieval Russia, power here lay not with a prince but with the veche, a city assembly, which elected officials and invited princes to serve as military leaders.

The old centre is a World Heritage site. The Kremlin, a brick fortress with a ring of walls and towers, stands on the left bank, and inside it rises the Cathedral of St Sophia, built in the eleventh century and one of the oldest stone buildings in Russia, with its helmet-shaped domes. Across the river, the market side holds Yaroslav's Court and a scatter of old churches. Archaeologists have found hundreds of birch-bark letters here, preserved in the damp soil, shopping lists, love notes and complaints written by ordinary people eight hundred years ago, and the museum has a good collection.

The city was nearly destroyed in the Second World War, and its churches were rebuilt carefully from ruins. A large monument in the Kremlin celebrates a thousand years of Russia, unveiled in 1862, with sculptures of historical figures around it. Walks along the river bank at dusk, with the Kremlin walls lit and the water quiet, are the best way to see the place.

The road from Valdai, the old tsarist route between Moscow and St Petersburg, is a pleasure, running through gentle forest and farmland, with the pace set by trucks and local cars. The surface varies, with some very good stretches and some old, patched ones, and speed cameras are common. The region has wide skies, low hills and large lakes, with the best riding in late spring and early autumn. Winter closes in with deep snow and ice.

Veliky Novgorod is a city of over two hundred thousand, so fuel, food and repairs are easy, with stations on all main roads. Pankovka and Volkhovsky are nearby suburbs with a few services. Local cuisine includes mushroom soups, fish from the lake and pies, and honey drinks have a long tradition here.

Allow time to wander on foot. The city is compact and rewards slow exploring, with a church around every corner.
t.managua@12.1,-86.2:
Managua is not an obvious beauty, and Nicaraguans will tell you so before you do. It lies on the southern shore of Lake Xolotlán, with the cone of the Momotombo volcano rising across the water, and its centre was destroyed by an earthquake in December 1972 that killed thousands. The old downtown was never rebuilt, and today the city sprawls in low neighbourhoods, with open lots, new roundabouts and the old cathedral standing cracked and empty as a reminder.

Several landmarks hold the story together. The Loma de Tiscapa, a hill over a crater lagoon, carries a huge silhouette of Sandino, the guerrilla leader who fought American occupation in the 1920s and 1930s, and the Palacio Nacional, with its neoclassical columns, houses a museum. The poet Rubén Darío, the father of modernist poetry in Spanish, is Nicaragua's national hero, and the national theatre bears his name. Managua is warm all year, and the rainy season from May to October brings heavy afternoon downpours.

Outside the city, the riding becomes better. To the south-east lie the Masaya volcano, where you can drive up to the rim of a smoking crater, and the colonial city of Granada beside Lake Nicaragua, with its yellow cathedral and painted houses. Laguna de Apoyo, a crater lake of warm blue water, is perfect for a swim. Northwest, the road leads toward León and the ruins of León Viejo, the first Spanish capital, abandoned after an earthquake and eruption in 1610 and buried under ash until excavation.

Traffic in Managua is chaotic, with buses, taxis, motorbikes and pedestrians, so ride defensively. Streets often lack names, and addresses are given by landmarks. Fuel is easy to find, and a plate of gallo pinto, rice and beans, with fried cheese and plantains, is a cheap breakfast. Keep valuables out of sight and park the bike in a guarded lot at night. The warmth of the people more than makes up for the city's plain face.
t.naqa@16.3,33.3:
Naqa stands in the dry grassland of the Butana, the steppe between the Nile and the Atbara in central Sudan, and it is one of the most surprising ruins in Africa. Two thousand years ago this was a prosperous town of the Kingdom of Kush, whose capital lay at Meroë, and its builders put up temples that mixed Egyptian, Greek, Roman and African ideas without any hesitation. The Temple of Apedemak, the lion-headed war god of the Kushites, has a front wall carved with a king and queen smiting enemies, and lions, snakes and gods crowding the sides. It is small, compact and very well preserved, and the sandstone glows orange in the late sun.

Next to it is the so-called Roman kiosk, a little building with Hathor-headed columns and arches that look as if a Mediterranean garden pavilion has been dropped into the Sudanese plain. A large temple to Amun stands facing a processional avenue of rams, which recalls the avenues of Karnak, but the animals here are carved in a more rustic style. The whole group of Naqa, Musawwarat es-Sufra and Meroë is now a World Heritage property.

The country is flat, semi-desert, with acacia, thorn scrub and seasonal streams that fill in the rains from July to September. In the dry season, the heat is intense, and dust can blow across the tracks. A road from the Nile and the main highway between Khartoum and Shendi leads off into the plain, with the last part on sand and gravel, and a guide is usually needed, since there are few signs and no services. Thorns are a real problem for tyres.

I should also be honest that Sudan has been at war since April 2023, with fighting around Khartoum and across much of the country, and travel there is not realistic at the moment. This text is about the place as it is remembered and recorded, and as it may be visited again when it is safe. Anyone planning a ride should consult up-to-date official advice and local sources, and not rely on old guides.
t.musawwarat es sufra@16.4,33.3:
Musawwarat es-Sufra sits in a shallow valley of the Butana, a few kilometres from the better-known temples of Naqa, and it is the most puzzling site of the Kushite kingdom. Instead of a town, it is a sprawling complex of sandstone courts, ramps, corridors and temples, known as the Great Enclosure, built from the third century BC onward. Archaeologists still argue about what it was for: a royal palace, a pilgrimage centre, a training place for elephants, a school for priests or something quite different. Its layout is a maze, with ramps instead of stairs, which suggests that animals may have been led through it, and the walls are decorated with carvings of elephants and other creatures.

The elephants are the thing visitors remember. A large stone elephant stands near the temple, carved in the round, and other animals appear in reliefs, which fits the evidence that Kush used war elephants and may have trained them here. The Lion Temple of Apedemak, a smaller building at the edge of the complex, was reconstructed in the twentieth century and shows the same lion god worshipped at Naqa. Graffiti scratched by visitors over the centuries, including Meroitic script, still cover some of the walls. The site is a World Heritage property, along with Naqa and Meroë.

The land around is open grassland and thorn scrub that turns green briefly in the rainy season and is dry and pale the rest of the year. Wadis cut across the plain, and the rock outcrops are made of the same sandstone the temples used. Shendi, the nearest large town at about thirty kilometres, lies on the Nile, and the main tarmac road between there and Khartoum offers a fast, straight ride through desert, with trucks and buses as the main hazard. The tracks to the site itself are sand and gravel and need caution, with no signs and no services.

Take water, fuel and a spare tube, since the closest supplies are in Shendi. The heat from April to June is extreme. As Sudan has been in conflict since April 2023, travel there is not currently realistic, and any plans should wait for reliable official advice and a safe situation on the ground.
t.cappadocia@38.6,34.8:
Cappadocia is a high plateau in central Turkey where two volcanoes, Erciyes and Hasan, once covered the land in ash, and where the wind and rain have since carved that soft rock into a landscape of cones, towers and ridges. The locals call the pointed pillars fairy chimneys, and some of them stand twenty metres tall, topped with a cap of harder stone. The rock is easy to dig, and for thousands of years people have cut homes, churches, storerooms and pigeon lofts into it, so that whole hillsides are riddled with doorways and windows, and some of the valleys look inhabited by ghosts.

Göreme, a village of a few thousand people, is the usual base, a cluster of cave houses and small hotels in a valley of pink and cream rock. Early Christians arrived in the first centuries and, during the long years of Arab raids and later iconoclasm, carved chapels with painted ceilings into the cliffs. Many of the frescoes still survive in the Göreme open-air museum nearby, and the colours of the saints' robes, in red, blue and ochre, are a surprise inside the dim stone rooms. Further afield, villages like Uçhisar, with its huge castle rock, and Avanos, famous for pottery made from the red clay of the Kızılırmak river, make good stops.

At dawn the sky fills with hot-air balloons, dozens or hundreds of them rising from the valleys in the first light, and it is one of the sights that justifies the early alarm. For motorcyclists the area is a delight, with well-surfaced roads that wind between valleys, rise over low ridges and drop through villages, and long views across a landscape of strange shapes. Traffic is moderate, though tour buses and quad bikes are common near the main sights. In summer the heat is dry and strong, with cool nights, and in winter the plateau gets snow and sharp frost, which makes the roads icy in the early morning.

Göreme and nearby towns such as Ürgüp and Avanos have fuel, cafes and workshops, so planning is easy. Pottery kebab, a stew sealed in a clay pot that the waiter cracks open at your table, is the local dish, and the local wines from Ürgüp are surprisingly good.
t.subterranean city of derinkuyu@38.4,34.8:
Derinkuyu means deep well, and the town above the underground city is named for it. Beneath the plain of Cappadocia, south of Nevşehir, people have carved a maze of tunnels, rooms, stables, kitchens, chapels, wine presses and storerooms to a depth of some sixty metres, over many levels, though only the upper eight or so are open to visitors. At its busiest the city could shelter thousands of people along with their animals and food stores. Large round stone doors, shaped like millstones, could be rolled across the passages from the inside to block intruders, and narrow shafts supplied air and water, so that a community could live below ground for months.

The origins are unclear. Soft volcanic rock was dug here from very early times, and the Hittites and Phrygians may have started the work, but the main use of the complex belongs to the Byzantine period, when Christians took refuge from raids during the Arab-Byzantine wars. Later, villagers used the rooms for storage and shelter, until the memory was nearly lost. The modern find is said to have come when a local man, renovating his house in the 1960s, knocked through a wall and found a room that led on into a passage, a story that may be partly legend but makes a good tale.

Moving through the tunnels is an odd experience, since the passages are low and tight, so you must stoop and sometimes squeeze. The air is cool and constant, around ten degrees, and the walls are smooth with age. It is not a place for anyone who dislikes enclosed spaces, but guides keep a steady pace and the route is lit. Visit early or late to avoid the tour buses, which fill the corridors in the middle of the day.

The ride south from Göreme and Nevşehir crosses open plateau, with wide, fast roads, fields of wheat and potato and a few poplar-lined villages. The traffic includes lorries and farm vehicles, and the wind can be strong in the open stretches. Derinkuyu has about twelve thousand people and has fuel, cafes and shops, and the neighbouring underground city of Kaymaklı lies roughly nine kilometres north. Snow in winter can close the minor roads, and summer afternoons are hot and dry.
t.goreme national park@38.7,34.9:
The national park around Göreme is the part of Cappadocia where the geology is most generous. Two great volcanoes, Erciyes and Hasan, buried the plateau in ash and lava millions of years ago, and the ash settled into a soft rock called tuff, which is cut by rivers and wind into valleys with names that sound invented: Love Valley, with its rows of phallic pillars, Rose Valley, which turns pink in the evening, Red Valley, Pigeon Valley and Sword Valley. Paths run through them, past orchards of apricot and apple, cave churches and the doorways of old dwellings, and on a good day you can hike for hours without meeting another person.

People have lived in the rock here for so long that the landscape is partly a work of architecture. Rooms are dug into the cones, with windows and steps cut in the stone, and the pigeon houses are carved into the cliffs with rows of tiny openings. The birds were valued for their droppings, which were used to fertilise vines and fields. At the Göreme Open Air Museum, a group of monastic churches and refectories shows how the monks lived in the tenth to twelfth centuries, and the painted ceilings and walls are among the finest Byzantine art in Anatolia. The Dark Church, which has its frescoes in rich colour because little light has ever reached them, is worth the extra ticket.

Riding in the park is a pleasure on the roads that wind between the villages, with good tarmac, gentle gradients and constant views. Many of the paths are for walkers only, and the tracks that look tempting are often sandy or full of loose gravel, so keep to the roads unless you have off-road experience. Heat in July and August can be fierce, with a dry wind and dust, and the nights cool quickly. Winter can bring snow and ice, and the stone gives the whole valley a hard, white look.

Göreme, about three kilometres away, has fuel nearby and plenty of cafes, and Avanos, five kilometres off, has bigger shops. Be at a viewpoint at dawn to see the balloons rise, and then have a Turkish breakfast with honey and clotted cream at a terrace restaurant.
t.konya@37.9,32.5:
Konya lies on the dry central plateau of Anatolia, about a thousand metres above the sea, and it has been an important city for as long as anyone has kept records. The Seljuk Turks made it their capital in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and it became a centre of learning and Sufi mysticism, the home of Jalal ad-Din Rumi, the poet and teacher who is known in Turkey as Mevlana. After his death in 1273 his followers founded the Mevlevi order, whose members perform the whirling ceremony, the sema, in which dancers in tall felt hats and white skirts turn slowly with one palm raised and one lowered. His tomb, under a fluted dome covered in turquoise tiles, is the most visited shrine in the country, and the pilgrims who gather there at all hours give the city a quiet devotional tone.

The city has other Seljuk monuments, including the Alaeddin Mosque on its hill and the Karatay Medrese, whose domed hall is covered in tile work in blue and turquoise. Conservative and proud of it, Konya is a place where bakeries sell etli ekmek, a long flat bread topped with minced lamb, and where the evening streets are calm. About forty kilometres south-east, on the plain, lies Çatalhöyük, a settlement of mud-brick houses entered from the roof, inhabited some nine thousand years ago and now a World Heritage site.

For a rider the surrounding country is vast, flat and bare. Roads run dead straight across steppe, with grain fields, poplars and the occasional grey village, and the sky is huge. Crosswinds can be strong, the summer sun is relentless, and in winter the plateau can be icy and snow-swept, with real cold. Distances between settlements are long, so keep an eye on fuel. To the west the lake of Beyşehir is a pleasant day trip, with mountains behind, and to the north-east, on the road toward Aksaray, the huge Seljuk caravanserai at Sultanhanı still shows what a medieval roadside stop looked like.

Konya is a big city with every service, and fuel stations are everywhere around it. The traffic inside the ring road is dense, but outside it the roads open quickly. A glass of tea in a courtyard near the Mevlana museum is the proper pause.
t.serengeti national park@-2.3,34.6:
Serengeti comes from the Maasai word siringet, meaning the place where the land runs on forever, and that is exactly the impression of the plains in northern Tanzania. Grassland stretches to the horizon, broken by granite outcrops called kopjes, flat-topped acacias and the green lines of rivers, and above it all the sky changes by the hour. The park covers nearly fifteen thousand square kilometres and joins Kenya's Maasai Mara to the north, forming the setting for the great migration, in which well over a million wildebeest and hundreds of thousands of zebra and gazelle follow the rains in an enormous circuit, with lions, cheetahs, hyenas and crocodiles waiting along the route.

The animals are here because of the soil and the seasons. Volcanic ash from the nearby Ngorongoro highlands has enriched the southern plains, which grow short, nutritious grass, and the herds gather there to give birth in the early months of the year, with the calving peaking around February. By the dry season they have moved north and west, and the crossing of the Mara river is the most dramatic scene of the year. Further south, the Olduvai Gorge, on the edge of the park, is where the Leakeys found the bones of early humans, and the area is often called a cradle of humankind.

I should be plain about the riding: motorcycles are not allowed in Tanzania's national parks, so this is a place for a safari vehicle, a ranger and a guide, and not a bike. The roads to the park gates, from Arusha via the Ngorongoro highlands or from Mwanza on Lake Victoria, are a mixture of tarmac and gravel, and in the rainy seasons, roughly March to May and November, black cotton soil turns to glue. Dust, corrugations and animals on the road are common hazards, and fuel in the remote north is scarce.

There are no towns listed near the coordinates, and the park has a small number of fuel points at its main camps, so plan to carry or arrange fuel before entering. Park fees are high and must be paid in advance. Evenings on the plains smell of dust and woodsmoke, and the roaring of lions after dark is something that people remember all their lives.
t.valdai@58.0,33.2:
Valdai is a lake town on high, wet, wooded ground halfway between Moscow and Saint Petersburg, and for three centuries travellers have stopped here because they had to. The Valdai Hills, which are really more of a rolling upland about two hundred metres above sea level, are the birthplace of rivers: the Volga, the Western Dvina and the Dnieper all start within a short distance. The town of eighteen thousand sits on the shore of Lake Valdai, a deep, clear lake in a bowl of forest, and the surrounding national park protects a mix of pine, spruce and bog.

The lake's island holds the Iversky Monastery, founded in the 1650s by Patriarch Nikon, who wanted a place to rival the great Orthodox sites on Mount Athos and modelled the buildings on them. Its white walls and golden domes reflect in the water, and it is reached by a short boat ride or a causeway. Nikon later fell from power, but the monastery stayed and was restored after periods of neglect.

Valdai's other claim to fame is its bells. In the eighteenth century, craftsmen here cast small bronze bells for the horse-drawn mail coaches on the road between the capitals, and the bells became so closely connected with the town that they are still called Valdai bells. They rang on the harness of troikas, and a small museum shows how they were cast. You can buy a modern copy in a shop, and its sound is bright and clear, a ringing that carries across the lake.

The old Tsarist road, known as the Sovereigns' Road, ran through here, with post stations where horses were changed. The riding in the area is easy, along tree-lined roads past villages with wooden houses, over low hills, with lakes appearing and vanishing between the pines. The surface is mixed, with good asphalt on the main road and patches of rough tarmac on the lanes. Elk and deer are common at dusk, and trucks use the highway at speed.

There is fuel in town, and it is a good place for a meal, with fish from the lake, mushroom dishes in season and the sweet baked goods Russians love. Summer is warm and green, with swimming in the lake, and autumn colours are fine from mid September. In winter the snow lies deep and the lake freezes, which turns the whole landscape into a white silence.
t.leon cathedral@12.4,-86.9:
León is a hot, lively university town in the north-west of Nicaragua, and its cathedral is the most sensible reason to stop. The Basilica Cathedral of the Assumption, as it is formally known, is the largest cathedral in Central America, a vast white block that dominates the central square. Construction ran from the middle of the eighteenth century into the early nineteenth, a long project in a region where earthquakes and wars kept interfering, and the result mixes Baroque and neoclassical touches under a roof that glares in the sun.

That white roof is the best part. You can climb up to it, walk across the domes and look out over a flat city, the red tile of neighbouring roofs and, on a clear day, the chain of volcanoes that stands along the Pacific side of the country. The cathedral also holds the tomb of Rubén Darío, the poet who changed Spanish-language verse around the turn of the twentieth century and who is revered here almost like a saint. A lion statue guards the grave, which gives the whole thing a pleasant theatrical feel. The building and surrounding old centre are recognised by UNESCO.

León has always been the intellectual and often rebellious counterpart to conservative Granada, and the city carries murals and memorials from the revolution, as well as a good number of lively cafés, which exist thanks to the students. It is a good place for a cold drink and a plate of something local such as nacatamal, a heavy steamed corn parcel, or a cool fruit drink from a street stall. Beyond town you can see Cerro Negro, a young volcano that has erupted repeatedly in the last century and a half.

Riding in and out is a matter of city patience. The roads from Managua, around ninety kilometres south-east, are generally straight and fast, shared with trucks, buses and the occasional horse cart. Take care with potholes, speed bumps in villages and drivers who overtake with enthusiasm. Heat is the main challenge, so start early and drink often.

Fuel is easy in a city of this size, with several stations on the approaches. Park somewhere you can see the bike, ask a local to point out a safe spot, and give yourself at least an hour in the square and on the roof.
t.vyshny volochyok@57.6,34.6:
Vyshny Volochyok sits on the Tvertsa River in Tver Oblast, halfway between Moscow and St. Petersburg, and its name tells the story: a volok was a portage, a place where boats were dragged overland between two river systems. Here, the Tvertsa, which flows to the Volga, comes within a short distance of the Msta, which flows toward Lake Ilmen and the Baltic, and for centuries merchants hauled their goods across the gap. Peter the Great saw the possibility of a permanent link and ordered a system of canals and locks, completed in the early eighteenth century, which made it possible to travel by water from the Volga to the Neva.

That system, the Vyshny Volochyok Water Route, carried huge cargoes to the new capital and made the town rich. Stone locks, many of them still visible, and canals lined with old brick warehouses recall that period. A small museum in the town explains how the system worked, and in the old center you find some fine merchant houses and a cathedral. The town later became famous for its glass factory, and for decades it produced fine tableware and decorations.

The surroundings are low, wooded and watery, with the Valdai Hills rising to the north and a patchwork of lakes. The Sovereign's Road, the old highway between Moscow and St. Petersburg, passed this way, and some of its stations still stand. The modern roads are a mix of fast highway and smaller routes, with the main M10 carrying heavy traffic and trucks. Side roads offer quiet bends through fields and forests, with the occasional glimpse of a canal or an old wooden church. Spring brings flooding in the low areas, and autumn is brilliant with birch and aspen.

For riders, the practical side is easy. The town has about fifty thousand people, with fuel stations along the highway, supermarkets and cafes, and a few small hotels. It is a convenient stop on a long ride between the two capitals. The old locks and the canal are a short walk from the center and are best seen in the morning light.

Take time to stand on a lock and look at the stones. They were laid by hand more than three centuries ago, and they are still working.
t.staraya russa@58.0,31.4:
Staraya Russa lies just south of Lake Ilmen in Novgorod Oblast, and it is one of the oldest towns in the region, with a history that goes back to the tenth or eleventh century. Its name means Old Russa, to distinguish it from the nearby Novgorod, and it was built around the salt springs that rise in the area. Salt production was the town's main business for centuries, and the Novgorod merchants who controlled the trade grew rich. In the nineteenth century a mud and mineral water spa grew up beside the salt works, and it remains a health resort today.

The town's greatest literary association is with Fyodor Dostoevsky, who bought a house here in the 1870s and spent his summers in it for several years. He wrote much of The Brothers Karamazov in Staraya Russa, and the town appears in the novel as Skotoprigonyevsk. The house, a modest wooden building beside the Pererytitsa river, is now a museum, with the writer's study and furniture preserved. Walking along the river, with the same low bridges and willow trees, gives a sense of the life he knew. Much of the town was destroyed during the Second World War, when the front line ran through it for two years, and the center was rebuilt in the Soviet period.

The landscape is flat, green and watery, with marshes, small rivers and wide skies. Lake Ilmen, one of the largest lakes in Russia, lies a short distance north, and in spring the river floods across the fields. The roads are mostly modest, with gentle curves and frost heaves, and summer traffic is light. The Valdai Hills rise to the east, offering more varied riding. Autumn is a fine season, with golden birch and clear air.

Practical help is easy to find. The town of about thirty-four thousand has fuel stations, a number of shops and cafes, and a few hotels or spa guesthouses. It is a comfortable place to stop between Novgorod and Valdai. Mosquitoes can be thick in summer near the water.

If you stop at the Dostoevsky house, ask to see the garden. The writer is said to have loved it, and the quiet there is the same as in his time.
t.kabale@-1.2,30.0:
Kabale is a hill town at about nineteen hundred metres in the far south-west of Uganda, and the first thing you notice is how cool it is. After the heat of Kampala and the lowlands, evenings here call for a jumper. The surrounding countryside, known as Kigezi, is a tight patchwork of terraces, so steep and so carefully cultivated that early colonial visitors compared it to Switzerland, and the nickname has stuck. Potatoes, sorghum, beans and cabbages are grown on slopes that look too steep to stand on.

The town itself is a bustling market centre of some forty thousand people, with a busy main street, crowded minibuses, shops selling everything from hardware to mobile phones, and a good number of small hotels. It is close to the Rwandan border at Katuna, and the Kisoro area, near the Virunga volcanoes and the corner where Uganda, Rwanda and the Congo meet, lies about thirty-four kilometres away on the western side. A few kilometres outside town is Lake Bunyonyi, a deep, finger-shaped lake dotted with small islands, and a lovely place to spend an afternoon.

Riding in the highlands is quite different from the flat plains. The roads climb and drop in long loops, switchback after switchback, between hills and valleys, with sudden views of terraces and mist. Surfaces are patchy, with sealed roads between the main towns but red murram, a compacted laterite dirt, on many side routes. The murram turns slick as soap in the rain, which here can be heavy and sudden, so keep speed down and be careful in the corners. Boda-bodas, the motorcycle taxis, are everywhere and ride with great confidence, so keep a wide margin and watch for pedestrians, cattle and children.

Fuel is not an issue in town, with several stations, but fill up before you head into the more remote parts, since stations thin out quickly. Eat matoke, the steamed green banana, with groundnut sauce, or a rolex, an egg rolled in a chapati, from a street stall. The dry seasons, from June to August and from December to February, are the easiest for riding. At other times, expect mud and a good chance of a soaking, and carry waterproofs and a cloth for the visor.
t.panorama route point 1@-24.9,30.8:
Graskop clings to the very edge of the Drakensberg escarpment, a small town that looks out over the Lowveld from a height of well over a thousand metres. Below, the land falls away in forested ravines to the plains that run all the way to the Kruger National Park. On a clear morning you can see far enough to understand why this stretch of road is called the Panorama Route.

The town has a past tied to gold. In the 1870s prospectors came to the nearby Pilgrim's Rest, a few kilometres north, and Graskop became a stop for wagons, miners and later the foresters who planted the pine and eucalyptus plantations that now cover much of the hills. Today it is a place for holidaymakers, with craft shops, small cafes and a long tradition of pancakes, which have become something of a local obsession. Order one with a savoury filling, as a lunch, and you will be in good company with half the other riders on this road.

The riding here is a pleasure, with long climbs through plantation forest, swinging curves above the escarpment and cool mist that can drift across the road in the early morning. The R532 and R533 are well surfaced but narrow in places, and tour buses and trucks make passing a task for patient riders. Be careful on damp mornings: the tar is smooth and the shade of the pines can hide patches of wet. Early starts reward you with empty roads and crisp air, while afternoons often bring cloud and thunderstorms in summer.

Graskop is a good town for practical stops. Fuel is available, there are banks and shops, and a number of guesthouses give you a place to sleep before tackling the viewpoints. A short walk from the main street leads to a gorge with a suspension bridge and lift, which is a modern attraction added to a place already famous for its views. Do not wear your full leathers for the walk, because it is humid.

Most travellers pass through quickly on their way to the better-known sights, but it pays to give Graskop an hour. The town marks the start of one of the best motorcycle roads in the country, with a string of waterfalls, canyons and viewpoints that unfold north and east of here. Fill the tank, eat well, and then ride toward God's Window and the Blyde River Canyon while the light is still good.
t.panorama route point 2@-24.9,30.9:
East of Graskop the plateau comes to a sudden end. The road leaves the grassland and plantations behind and begins to fall toward the Lowveld, a drop of hundreds of metres in a few kilometres, with views opening between the trees and the air getting noticeably warmer as you descend. On this side of the escarpment the climate changes from cool highveld to subtropical bush, and you can feel it on your skin before the thermometer agrees.

The rivers draw the eye here. Close to Graskop, the Lisbon and Berlin Falls drop off the escarpment edge into forested gorges, and the water feeds streams that run down toward the Sabie and Blyde catchments. Short walks from the car parks lead to viewpoints, and the roar of the falls grows louder as you approach. In the rainy summer months they run full, brown with soil, and the mist from them can sit above the treetops.

For riders the interest is the descent itself. The roads that tumble off the escarpment, including the famous Kowyn's Pass on the way to Hazyview, wind down through tight bends with steep banks and tall trees. The surface is generally good, but leaf litter, wet patches and occasional loose gravel on corners deserve respect, and slow trucks on the descent are common. Use engine braking rather than leaning on the front brake, and watch for baboons and monkeys that sit by the verge looking for handouts.

The Lowveld below is hotter, drier and busier. Citrus orchards, banana plantations and small farming towns line the roads, and there are craft markets, curio stalls and fruit sellers beside the tar. The nearest larger town with proper services listed in our data is Thulamahashi, about thirty-six kilometres away, but most riders find fuel and food in Hazyview or back in Graskop, where the choice is better. Fill up before you commit to a long section of the escarpment, because the garages are spaced further apart than you might like.

Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms, usually rolling in around three or four o'clock with cracks of lightning over the escarpment and sudden downpours that turn the road to a river for ten minutes. Start early, get your viewpoints done by midday, and be somewhere dry with a cold drink when the cloud builds. In winter the days are clear and dry, the grass turns the colour of straw, and the air can be cold at the top and warm at the bottom.
t.panorama route point 3@-24.7,30.8:
Bourke's Luck Potholes is one of those places where water has done something so tidy that it looks designed. At the meeting of the Treur and Blyde rivers, the current has spent thousands of years swirling pebbles and grit against the sandstone and dolomite, carving cylindrical hollows in the rock that look like giant cooking pots. A footbridge crosses the gorge so you can look down into the swirling pools from above, and the colour of the water, a deep green over pale stone, makes a surprisingly good photograph.

The names tell the story. Treur means mourning in Afrikaans, and Blyde means joyful. A group of Voortrekkers camped by the river in the nineteenth century, and when the men who had gone ahead returned safely, the party renamed the second river in celebration. The potholes themselves are named after a gold prospector, Tom Bourke, who staked a claim here and, so the story goes, never found the fortune he expected. That kind of irony is common in this part of Mpumalanga, where gold rushes came and went in the 1870s.

Getting here is half the fun. The R532 north of Graskop passes God's Window and the road then runs along the top of the escarpment, rolling through grassland and patches of forest before dropping gently to the car park. The surface is generally excellent, the corners are open and flowing, and traffic is light outside of school holidays, though tour buses stop at every viewpoint. The air is cool at this height, and mist is common, particularly in the morning, so a light jacket is worthwhile even in summer.

Nature is part of the pleasure. The canyon walls are home to baboons, klipspringers and a range of birds including the Cape vulture, which nests on the cliffs and can be seen soaring on thermals in the afternoon. The vegetation changes quickly with altitude, from grassland to forest to the aloes that flower orange and red in winter, giving the rocks a splash of colour.

Graskop, about thirty kilometres south, is the sensible place to fill up, and most riders plan their stop here as a walk of an hour or so before moving on to the viewpoints at the Three Rondavels. Watch the rocks near the railings, because the spray from the falls makes them slippery, and keep your helmet and gloves in a safe place when you cross the bridge.
t.panorama route point 4@-24.6,30.8:
Few places on the Panorama Route justify the superlatives as well as the Blyde River Canyon rim. The canyon is one of the largest green canyons in the world, in the sense that subtropical vegetation covers its walls rather than bare rock, and it runs for tens of kilometres along the northern end of the Drakensberg escarpment. From the viewpoint car parks the red cliffs fall away to the river, the Blydepoort Dam and the reeds along the shore.

The three round, thatched-hut-shaped peaks on the far side of the canyon are known as the Three Rondavels, a name that comes from the traditional round houses of the region. They stand high over the water, and on a clear morning the light turns them a warm rust colour against the green below. Cloud often sits in the valley, and when it clears the view changes minute by minute, so a patient stop of half an hour can give you a very different photograph from a quick look.

The riding that links these viewpoints is gentle, with long open bends, a smooth surface and a lot of room, but you must stay alert. Tourist cars stop suddenly at the lookouts, there are vendors on the verge selling carvings and crystals, and in damp weather the cloud can drop visibility to a few metres. Come in the morning if you can, ideally on a weekday, when the light is soft and the car parks are quiet. Summer brings thunderstorms in the afternoon and a risk of lightning on the exposed ridge.

The nature here is rich. The canyon sits in the Blyde River Canyon Nature Reserve, and its slopes shelter hippos in the dam, crocodiles in the river and a wide range of antelope and birds. The cliffs hold a colony of Cape vultures, and the aloes along the rim flower in winter, filling the air with sunbirds. The rock is mostly sandstone and quartzite, and the colours range from yellow to deep red.

Small stalls and a simple cafe or two serve cold drinks and snacks, and there are guesthouses in the area if you prefer to linger for the sunset. Pay the small entrance fee where asked, keep your belongings out of sight when parked, and give the baboons a wide berth.
t.panorama route point 5@-24.6,30.8:
The northern end of the canyon rim is where the Panorama Route begins to lose its altitude, and the road starts the long drop toward the Lowveld and the town of Hoedspruit. These coordinates sit in that landscape, and the feel of the place is of a mountain wall slowly giving way to bushveld, with the temperatures rising as the road falls.

For a rider the best part of this section is the descent through the Abel Erasmus Pass area, where the R36 winds through a sequence of bends beside tall rock faces and between patches of bush. The road surface is mostly good, the traffic includes slow-moving trucks and tour vehicles, and there are tunnels and cuttings that can be shadowed and cool even on a hot day. Take it steadily, and be ready for a sudden sharp bend after a long straight, because the road designers here never seemed to trust the landscape.

The land beyond the escarpment has long been a corridor between the highveld and the coast. Early traders, gold seekers and later settlers all used the passes around here, and some of the old routes are still visible as tracks and cuttings beside the modern road. Names such as Abel Erasmus remind you of the nineteenth-century officials who policed the region, while the Pedi and the Swazi had walked these slopes long before the first wagons.

The wildlife begins to change as you go down. Instead of grassland and forest you will see acacia and marula trees, and you may spot vervet monkeys, baboons and the occasional antelope by the roadside. Near the foot of the escarpment the private game reserves that border Kruger National Park begin, and the smell of warm bush and dust is quite different from the damp forest up above. Keep your speed measured at dusk, because animals can step into the road with little warning.

On the practical side, fuel is available in Hoedspruit, which is the largest town nearby and a sensible refill point after the climb and descent, and it also has supermarkets, restaurants and a good selection of accommodation. There are few services on the escarpment road itself, so do not rely on finding a petrol station on the way. If you plan to continue into the Kruger, remember that the gates close at fixed hours, so plan your arrival with the clock in mind and watch the light, which fades quickly in the subtropics.
